knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Functional Convex MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable functional formulation with convex continuous restrictions for each integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A smooth functional convex MINLP has the form 
\[\inf\{f(x,y):g_i(x,y)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\},\]
where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\). For every \(y\in Y\), the functions \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) and \(x\mapsto g_i(x,y)\) are finite, convex, and continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\). Consequently, at any \(\bar x\in X\), their gradients define valid affine global underestimators in the continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex MINLP has integer variables and differentiable convex objective and constraint functions in the continuous variables, whose gradients generate valid affine underestimators.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\).
For each \(y\in Y\), all functional terms are convex and continuously differentiable near \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(x,y)\ge h(\bar x,y)+\nabla_x h(\bar x,y)^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) for each functional term \(h\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Functional Convex MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional formulation admitting nondifferentiable convex terms and subgradient support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonsmooth functional convex MINLP has the form
\[\inf\{f(x,y):g_i(x,y)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\},\]
where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex, \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\), and, for every fixed \(y\in Y\), the functions \(f(\cdot,y)\) and \(g_i(\cdot,y)\) are proper convex functions on \(X\), without a differentiability requirement. If \(s\in\partial_x h(\bar x,y)\), then \(h(x,y)\ge h(\bar x,y)+s^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) for every \(x\in X\), providing oracle-based affine support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth convex MINLP uses proper convex continuous-variable functions; any available subgradient supplies a globally valid affine support inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\).
For fixed \(y\), each functional term is proper and convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\in\partial_x h(\bar x,y)\Rightarrow h(x,y)\ge h(\bar x,y)+s^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) for all \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential with respect to the continuous variables

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Representable Convex MINLP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted cone-native representation of mixed-integer convex feasible sets and objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex MINLP is conic-representable when, after introducing auxiliary continuous variables \(z\), it can be written as
\[\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}y+e^{\mathsf T}z:Ax+By+Cz-b\in K,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ y\in Y,\ z\in\mathbb R^q\},\]
where \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) and \(K\) is a closed convex cone. Projecting the lifted conic feasible set onto \((x,y)\) recovers the original feasible set, and the lifted linear objective has the same infimum. Polyhedral interfaces correspond to polyhedral \(K\); nonlinear convex interfaces arise by expressing convex epigraphs through cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic interface lifts the MINLP into affine membership in a closed convex cone, preserving feasibility under projection and preserving the optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The lifted formulation projects exactly onto the original feasible set and preserves objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}\{(x,y,z):Ax+By+Cz-b\in K\}=F\), with equal original and lifted infima.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is plausible and locally appropriate, but no source is supplied for the exact lifted conic representability and projection-preservation claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Integer Convex NLP Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric family obtained by fixing the integer vector in a convex MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the convex MINLP
\[\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le 0,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\},\]
each assignment \(\bar y\in Y\) induces the continuous subproblem
\[P(\bar y):\quad v(\bar y)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x,\bar y):g(x,\bar y)\le 0\}.\]
If \(f(\cdot,\bar y)\) and every component of \(g(\cdot,\bar y)\) are convex and \(X\) is convex, then \(P(\bar y)\) is a convex optimization problem. The original MINLP value equals \(\inf_{y\in Y}v(y)\), using \(v(y)=+\infty\) for infeasible subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing each integer assignment produces a convex continuous subproblem, and minimizing their extended-real optimal values recovers the MINLP optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\).
For every \(y\in Y\), the objective and constraint functions are convex in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{MINLP}}=\inf_{y\in Y}v(y)\), where infeasibility implies \(v(y)=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: continuous convex subproblem indexed by an integer assignment

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Convex Relaxation View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound obtained by replacing the discrete domain with a convex continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[v_I=\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le0,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\}\]
be a minimization convex MINLP, and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) be convex with \(Y\subseteq R\). Its continuous relaxation has value
\[v_R=\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le0,\ x\in X,\ y\in R\}.\]
Whenever the functions are jointly convex on \(X\times R\), the relaxed problem is convex. Because its feasible set contains the mixed-integer feasible set, \(v_R\le v_I\). Equality holds if a relaxed optimizer has \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing the integer domain to a convex superset gives a convex lower-bounding problem; the bound is exact when a relaxed optimum is integral.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
\(Y\subseteq R\), with \(X\times R\) convex and all functional terms jointly convex there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_R\le v_I\), with \(v_R=v_I\) if a relaxation optimizer has \(y\in Y\).

notation.meaning: convex relaxation of the integer domain

children.title: Projected Master-Space View
children.top_down_role: Discrete-space value and feasibility geometry induced by continuous optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Master-Space View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete projection described by feasibility and value functions induced by continuous optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a mixed-integer convex model, define the projected feasible domain and value function by
\[D=\{y\in Y:\exists x\in X,\ g(x,y)\le0\},\qquad v(y)=\inf\{f(x,y):x\in X,\ g(x,y)\le0\}.\]
Extend \(v(y)=+\infty\) for \(y\notin D\). The original problem is equivalently
\[\inf_{y\in Y}v(y)=\inf_{y\in D}v(y).\]
Thus a master-space formulation may operate only in \(y\), using lower models of \(v\) and constraints that outer-approximate or exactly describe \(D\); continuous subproblems evaluate or separate candidate master points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting out continuous variables yields a discrete feasible domain and an extended-real value function; optimizing that function is equivalent to the original MINLP.
assumptions_latex: The extended-real convention assigns \(+\infty\) to infeasible fixed-integer subproblems.
Each fixed-integer subproblem is interpreted over the same continuous set \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{MINLP}}=\inf_{y\in Y}v(y)=\inf_{y\in D}v(y)\).

notation.meaning: projection of the feasible set onto the integer variables

knowledge_statements.title: Complicating-Integer Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A discrete block whose fixation exposes a tractable continuous convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A MINLP has complicating-integer structure relative to \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) if it can be written as
\[\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le0,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\},\]
and, for every fixed \(\bar y\in Y\), the residual problem in \(x\) is a tractable convex optimization problem, while the unfixed model retains the discrete coupling through \(y\). In particular, \(X\) is convex and \(f(\cdot,\bar y)\) and all components of \(g(\cdot,\bar y)\) are convex. Decomposition may therefore enumerate, relax, or cut in the \(y\)-space while solving convex subproblems in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integers are complicating when fixing them leaves a tractable convex continuous problem, enabling a discrete master coupled to continuous subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) and \(X\) is convex.
Every fixed-\(y\) residual problem is convex and belongs to the stipulated tractable solver class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=\bar y\) reduces the MINLP to a tractable convex optimization problem in \(x\).

children.title: Block-Separable Convex MINLP
children.top_down_role: Convex blocks coupled by a smaller linking structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Convex MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex local blocks joined through a lower-dimensional linking system and shared integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A block-separable convex MINLP admits a formulation
\[\inf\left\{\sum_{k=1}^K f_k(x_k,y):x_k\in X_k,\ g_k(x_k,y)\le0,\ \sum_{k=1}^K A_kx_k+By=b,\ y\in Y\right\},\]
where \(K\in\mathbb N\), \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\), every \(X_k\) is convex, and, for each fixed \(y\in Y\), each \(f_k(\cdot,y)\) and every component of \(g_k(\cdot,y)\) is convex. Apart from the displayed affine linking equation and the shared integer vector \(y\), variables from distinct blocks do not occur in the same objective or constraint term. Thus, after fixing \(y\), the affine linking equation is the only remaining cross-block coupling; removing, allocating, or dualizing that equation yields independent convex block problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model consists of convex local blocks coupled only through shared integers and an affine linking equation. Once the integers are fixed, that equation is the sole remaining cross-block coupling, and treating it by removal, allocation, or dualization separates the blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb N\), each \(X_k\) is convex, and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\).
For each fixed \(y\in Y\), all block objective and inequality functions are convex in their local variables.
No objective or constraint term other than the displayed linking equation contains variables from more than one block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(y\), \(\sum_{k=1}^K A_kx_k+By=b\) is the only remaining cross-block coupling; treating this equation by removal, allocation, or dualization separates the continuous problem into \(K\) convex block problems.

notation.meaning: block contribution to the affine linking equation

children.title: Design–Operation Structure
children.top_down_role: Discrete design choices coupled with convex operational subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Design–Operation Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete design decisions parameterize a convex operational value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A design–operation convex MINLP has the two-level representation
\[\inf_{y\in Y}\{c(y)+Q(y)\},\qquad Q(y)=\inf_{x\in X(y)}\{q(x,y):g(x,y)\le0\},\]
where \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) contains design choices and \(x\) contains operational decisions. For every fixed admissible design \(y\), the set \(\{x\in X(y):g(x,y)\le0\}\) is convex and \(q(\cdot,y)\) is convex. The convention \(Q(y)=+\infty\) represents an operationally infeasible design. Hence the design master minimizes capital cost plus the convex operational subproblem value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer design choices determine convex operational subproblems; the master minimizes design cost plus the operational value, with infeasible designs assigned infinite value.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) is the admissible design set.
For every fixed \(y\), the operational feasible set and objective are convex in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v=\inf_{y\in Y}\{c(y)+Q(y)\}\), with \(Q(y)=+\infty\) for operational infeasibility.

children.title: Scenario-Recourse Coupling
children.top_down_role: Discrete master decisions coupled to separable convex scenario subproblems.

children.title: Scenario Organization
children.top_down_role: Indexing, separability, probability weighting, plus shared structure across scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Organization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario organization with shared first-stage decisions and scenario-local recourse blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite scenario set \(S\), a scenario-organized convex MINLP is represented by
\[\inf_{y\in Y,\,x_s}\left\{c(y)+\sum_{s\in S}p_s q_s(x_s,y):g_s(x_s,y)\le0,\ x_s\in X_s,\ s\in S\right\},\]
where \(p_s\ge0\), \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\), and \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) is shared across scenarios. Each \(x_s\) and its constraints are local to scenario \(s\). For fixed \(y\), convexity of every local feasible set and \(q_s(\cdot,y)\) makes the recourse blocks independently solvable by scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-scenario model shares first-stage integers across scenario-local convex recourse blocks and aggregates their values with scenario weights.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(p_s\ge0\), and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
For fixed \(y\), every scenario block is a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(y\), the minimization over \((x_s)_{s\in S}\) separates into independent scenario subproblems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-scenario organization and fixed-design separability claim are mathematically plausible, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the stochastic-programming representation.

children.title: Recourse Subproblem Structure
children.top_down_role: Convex recourse models induced by fixed discrete master decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Subproblem Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-local convex optimization induced by a fixed first-stage integer decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a first-stage decision \(\bar y\in Y\) and scenario \(s\in S\), the recourse subproblem is
\[Q_s(\bar y)=\inf_{x_s\in X_s}\{q_s(x_s,\bar y):g_s(x_s,\bar y)\le0\}.\]
It is a convex recourse subproblem when \(X_s\) is convex and, for fixed \(\bar y\), the objective \(q_s(\cdot,\bar y)\) and all constraint functions \(g_{sj}(\cdot,\bar y)\) are convex. Set \(Q_s(\bar y)=+\infty\) if the scenario is infeasible and \(Q_s(\bar y)=-\infty\) if it is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing a first-stage decision and a scenario yields a convex recourse problem whose extended-real value records feasibility and boundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(X_s\) is convex.
For fixed \(\bar y\), \(q_s\) and every component of \(g_s\) are convex in \(x_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s(\bar y)\) is the extended-real optimal value of a convex scenario subproblem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex scenario subproblem and extended-real conventions are coherent, but no authoritative recourse-definition source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Scenario–Recourse Coupling
children.top_down_role: Linking architecture between master decisions plus scenario-specific recourse components.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario–Recourse Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipative first-stage decisions couple otherwise separable scenario recourse problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With scenario recourse values \(Q_s(y)\), the coupled finite-scenario problem is
\[\inf_{y\in Y}\left\{c(y)+\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(y)\right\}.\]
Equivalently, introduce scenario copies \(y_s\) and a common vector \(z\), impose \(y_s=z\) for every \(s\in S\), and solve the scenario blocks in \((y_s,x_s)\). These nonanticipativity equations are the sole cross-scenario coupling when all other variables and constraints are scenario-local. Removing them yields independent scenario problems but generally permits different first-stage decisions and therefore changes the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario recourse blocks are coupled by a common nonanticipative first-stage decision; scenario copies make this coupling explicit through consensus equations.
assumptions_latex: All second-stage variables and constraints are scenario-local.
A single first-stage decision must be chosen before the scenario is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_s=z\) for all \(s\in S\) is equivalent to using one shared nonanticipative decision \(y\).

notation.meaning: scenario copy of the first-stage decision

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the nonanticipativity representation, and the common vector z is not assigned a domain. Exact equivalence requires the scenario copies and consensus vector to share the admissible first-stage domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,p,m,r\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(Z\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\), and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{r\times p}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^r\). Consider minimizing \(f(x,z)\) subject to \(g_i(x,z)\le 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(Ax+Bz=b\), \(x\in X\), and \(z\in Z\). The model has explicit global convexity when, for every \(z\in Z\), the functions \(f(\cdot,z)\) and \(g_i(\cdot,z)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are proper convex functions on \(X\). Consequently, for every \(z\in Z\), the continuous feasible set \(C_z=\{x\in X:g_i(x,z)\le0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ Ax+Bz=b\}\) is convex, and every affine inequality obtained from a valid global support of a defining convex function is valid on that fixed-integer slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A MINLP has explicit global convexity when every fixed-integer continuous subproblem has a convex objective and a convex feasible set represented by specified convex inequalities and affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature of a bivariate integer-power monomial on sign-restricted domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature classification on convex components of the sign-restricted region where the integer-power monomial is finite; the full set defined by xy≤0 need not itself be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x,y)=x^a y^b with a,b\in\mathbb Z. Suppose that (a,b are odd and xy\le 0), or (a is odd, b is even, and x\le 0), or (a is even, b is odd, and y\le 0). On each convex component of the corresponding region on which f is finite, f is concave if (a\le 0 and b\le 0), or (a\le 0 and 1-a-b\le 0), or (b\le 0 and 1-a-b\le 0). It is convex if a\ge 0, b\ge 0, and a+b\le 1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under any stated parity-and-sign regime, and away from points where a negative power is undefined, the monomial is concave under any of the three listed exponent conditions and convex when both exponents are nonnegative and sum to at most one. Curvature is understood on convex components of the sign-restricted domain.

f(x,y)=x^a y^b\text{ is finite on the domain considered}
\bigl(a,b\text{ odd}\land xy\le0\bigr)\lor\bigl(a\text{ odd}\land b\text{ even}\land x\le0\bigr)\lor\bigl(a\text{ even}\land b\text{ odd}\land y\le0\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}. knowledge_statements.title: Latent Convex Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity exposed only after an exact change of variables or lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed-integer feasible slice \(F_z\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has latent convex structure if there exist a convex set \(K_z\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), a map \(T_z:K_z\to F_z\), and a convex function \(\widehat f_z:K_z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \(T_z(K_z)=F_z\) and \(\widehat f_z(u)=f(T_z(u),z)\) for every \(u\in K_z\). For optimization equivalence, every feasible original point must have a preimage and objective values must be preserved; injectivity of \(T_z\) is unnecessary unless recovery of a unique lifted representative is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Latent convexity means an exact lifting or variable transformation converts each continuous slice into a convex problem while preserving feasibility and objective values.
assumptions_latex: The transformation and lifted set are defined for every fixed integer vector under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in F_z}f(x,z)=\inf_{u\in K_z}\widehat f_z(u)\).

notation.meaning: recovery map from lifted to original variables

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent sufficient definition of optimization equivalence, but an unrestricted surjective recovery map can encode essentially any feasible set and may not match an established meaning of latent convex structure. An authoritative source is needed to determine the intended transformation or lifting conditions.

children.title: Equivalent Convex Reformulations

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Convex Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization equivalence between an original slice and a convex extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_z\) be an original fixed-integer feasible set with objective \(f(\cdot,z)\). A convex extended formulation is equivalent when a convex set \(Q_z\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^r\) and convex objective \(\phi_z\) satisfy \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_z)=F_z\) and
\[f(x,z)=\inf\{\phi_z(x,w):(x,w)\in Q_z\}\quad\text{for every }x\in F_z.\]
Hence
\[\inf_{x\in F_z}f(x,z)=\inf_{(x,w)\in Q_z}\phi_z(x,w),\]
and projecting any attained reformulated optimizer yields an original optimizer. Equality only of optimal values is weaker and does not by itself establish formulation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended convex model is equivalent when its projection recovers exactly the original feasible set and partial minimization recovers the original objective pointwise.
assumptions_latex: The infima are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
Optimizer recovery is asserted only when the reformulated infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two formulations have equal optimal values, and attained reformulated solutions project to original optimal solutions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection and pointwise partial-minimization conditions are mathematically coherent and the representation kind fits the leaf, but no source supports this exact definition or its optimizer-recovery assertion.

children.title: Reformulation Validity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where the proposed representation changes feasibility, closure, or global validity.

knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Validity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness requirements separating valid convex reformulations from relaxations or restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an original feasible set \(F\) and proposed convex extended set \(Q\), exact feasibility requires \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=F\). If \(F\subsetneq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\), the construction is only a relaxation and may produce an infeasible projected optimizer; if \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\subsetneq F\), it is a restriction and may discard an optimizer. Even when projections agree, replacing \(f(x)\) by \(\inf\{\phi(x,w):(x,w)\in Q\}\) is valid only if these values equal \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Thus convexity of \(Q\) alone does not establish equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex reformulation ceases to be exact if projection changes feasibility or partial minimization changes any feasible point’s objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(Q\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of projection equality or pointwise objective recovery prevents certification of exact reformulation equivalence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is plausible and appropriately classified, but no cited source supports the precise projection and pointwise-objective exactness criteria.

children.title: Nonconvex Continuous-Structure Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Continuous-Structure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary beyond which local first-order NLP models are not global certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable constraint function \(g\), the affine model \(g(\bar x)+\nabla g(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) is a global underestimator only when the supporting inequality holds throughout the domain, as it does for convex \(g\). Without convexity, local linearization can remove feasible points: on \([-1,1]\), let \(g(x)=-x^2\) and impose \(g(x)\le-1/4\). At \(\bar x=1/2\), linearization gives \(-x+1/4\le-1/4\), or \(x\ge1/2\), although every \(x\in[-1,-1/2]\) is feasible. Such a cut is therefore not globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without continuous convexity, a tangent derived from local NLP information can exclude globally feasible points and cannot serve as a global outer-approximation cut.
assumptions_latex: The linearization is used as a replacement for a nonlinear inequality over the full domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local first-order information alone does not certify a globally valid outer model for nonconvex continuous constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order global support for differentiable convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable at \(\bar x\in U\). Then the affine function \[\ell_{\bar x}(x)=f(\bar x)+\nabla f(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\] satisfies \(\ell_{\bar x}(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in U\). Consequently, for an epigraph coordinate \(t\in\mathbb R\), the inequality \(t\ge\ell_{\bar x}(x)\) is valid for \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Intersecting finitely many such halfspaces gives a polyhedral outer approximation of the epigraph, equivalently a piecewise-affine lower model of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function on an open convex domain, the tangent at any point where the function is differentiable is a global affine underestimator and defines a valid epigraph cut.

children.title: Subgradient Support Models

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Support Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine support for possibly nonsmooth convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex, let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and choose \(s\in\partial f(\bar x)\). By the defining subgradient inequality,
\[f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+s^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
Thus \(t\ge f(\bar x)+s^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) is a globally valid linear inequality for \(\operatorname{epi}f\). A finite collection of subgradients produces the lower model \(m(x)=\max_j\{f(x^j)+s_j^{\mathsf T}(x-x^j)\}\), which satisfies \(m(x)\le f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every subgradient of a proper convex function defines a global affine underestimator; finitely many such supports form a polyhedral lower model.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex.
\(s\in\partial f(\bar x)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential at the reference point

children.title: Conic Separation Models

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Separation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear cuts certified by dual-cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone and consider the conic set \(S=\{x:Ax+b\in K\}\). For any \(y\in K^*=\{y:y^{\mathsf T}v\ge0\ \forall v\in K\}\), the inequality
\[y^{\mathsf T}(Ax+b)\ge0\]
is valid for every \(x\in S\). If a point \(\bar x\notin S\) admits \(y\in K^*\) with \(y^{\mathsf T}(A\bar x+b)<0\), then \(y\) is a directly verifiable separation certificate: dual-cone membership proves validity, while the strict inequality proves exclusion of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-cone vector produces a valid linear inequality for a conic feasible set and certifies separation when the candidate point violates it strictly.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The conic constraint is affine in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in K^*\) and \(y^{\mathsf T}(A\bar x+b)<0\) certify a valid cut separating \(\bar x\) from \(S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual-cone certificate is mathematically plausible and the certificate kind fits the leaf, but a generic convex-sets section is not adequate evidence for the dual-cone validity and strict-separation assertions. A conic duality or cone separation locator is required.

children.title: Closed Perspective Formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Perspective Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex hull representation for an activated convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, with recession function \(f^\infty\). Its closed perspective is
\[\widetilde f(x,z)=\begin{cases}z f(x/z),&z>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&z=0,\\ +\infty,&z<0.\end{cases}\]
This function is closed and convex. If the inactive state requires \(x=0\) and \(f^\infty(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\), then
\[\{(x,z,t):0\le z\le1,\ t\ge\widetilde f(x,z)\}\]
is the closed convex hull of the union of the inactive epigraph state \(\{(0,0,t):t\ge0\}\) and the active state \(\{(x,1,t):t\ge f(x)\}\), assuming \(f(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective extends an activated convex epigraph to zero activation using the recession function and, under stated conditions, gives its closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and \(f(0)=0\).
\(f^\infty(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epigraph of \(\widetilde f\) over \(0\le z\le1\) equals the closed convex hull of the inactive and active epigraph states.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation invokes a nontrivial closed-perspective convex-hull theorem and recession-boundary conditions. No source is supplied, so the exact hull statement cannot be accepted at candidate-review level.

children.title: Perspective-Cut Formulations
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral implementations of perspective strengthening.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective-Cut Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral outer approximation of a closed perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be closed convex with \(f(0)=0\), and let \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f\) admit \(s\in\partial f(u)\). The subgradient support \(f(v)\ge f(u)+s^{\mathsf T}(v-u)\), applied at \(v=x/z\) and multiplied by \(z>0\), yields the perspective cut
\[t\ge s^{\mathsf T}x+\bigl(f(u)-s^{\mathsf T}u\bigr)z.\]
The inequality remains valid for the closed perspective epigraph at \(z=0\). Intersecting such cuts for finitely many pairs \((u,s)\) gives a polyhedral relaxation of \(t\ge\widetilde f(x,z)\); it is exact only if the selected supports represent the perspective epigraph completely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling subgradient supports yields linear perspective cuts. Any finite collection is a valid polyhedral relaxation, but generally not an exact perspective formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed and convex with \(f(0)=0\).
\(s\in\partial f(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge s^{\mathsf T}x+(f(u)-s^{\mathsf T}u)z\) is valid whenever \(t\ge\widetilde f(x,z)\) and \(z\ge0\).

notation.meaning: support point in the unscaled variable space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled subgradient inequality is plausible and the representation kind fits the polyhedral formulation leaf, but validity at the zero-activation recession boundary and the exactness qualification require an authoritative perspective-reformulation source.

children.title: Perspective Conic Formulations
children.top_down_role: Cone-preserving extended representations of activated convex terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Conic Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-preserving homogenization of an activated conic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a closed convex epigraph has the conic representation
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(u,\tau):Fu+g\tau+h\in K\},\]
where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. Its homogenized perspective representation is
\[\{(x,z,t):Fx+gt+hz\in K,\ z\ge0\}.\]
For \(z>0\), conicity permits division by \(z\), so this constraint is equivalent to \((x/z,t/z)\in\operatorname{epi}f\), or \(t\ge zf(x/z)\). At \(z=0\), it represents the corresponding recession epigraph. Thus the formulation preserves the original cone family while extending the perspective closure to the inactive boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing the affine offset in a conic epigraph representation gives a cone-preserving formulation of the closed perspective, including its recession boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The displayed conic system represents the closed epigraph of \(f\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Fx+gt+hz\in K\), \(z\ge0\), represents the closed perspective epigraph induced by the given conic representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-activation homogenization follows formally from conicity, but the assertion that the zero-activation system exactly represents the closed recession epigraph is nontrivial and unsupported. A source specifying the required closedness or representability hypotheses is needed.

children.title: Indicator Convex Formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Convex Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact logical activation of a convex constraint by a binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, and let \(g:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex. The indicator constraint
\[z=1\ \Longrightarrow\ g(x)\le0\]
represents the disjunctive feasible set
\[\bigl(X\times\{0\}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\{x\in X:g(x)\le0\}\times\{1\}\bigr).\]
It is an exact logical formulation only when the solver enforces this implication globally. Replacing it by \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\) is equivalent only if \(M\) is a valid finite upper bound for \(g\) on \(X\); otherwise the replacement can exclude feasible inactive points or be undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary indicator activates a convex constraint exactly. A big-M replacement is equivalent only with a valid finite bound over the inactive domain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(g\) is convex on \(X\).
\(z\) is binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indicator implication exactly represents the displayed two-term disjunction; big-M equivalence additionally requires \(M\ge\sup_{x\in X}g(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed implication and disjunction agree, and the big-M bound condition is plausible, but no source supports the exact indicator semantics or the global finite-bound equivalence. The representation kind otherwise fits the leaf.

\(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
\(M\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(M\geq\sup_{x\in X}g(x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{(x,z)\in X\times\{0,1\}:g(x)\leq Mz\}\), and replacing \(z\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\leq z\leq1\) gives a convex relaxation.

notation.meaning: Valid finite upper bound on the constraint function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The convention is that \(z=0\) activates the convex constraint and \(z=1\) deactivates it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the implication “if \(z=0\), then \(g(x)\leq0\),” the inequality \(g(x)\leq Mz\) is valid and exact for binary \(z\): at \(z=0\) it imposes the constraint, while at \(z=1\) it is redundant on \(X\). Finiteness and validity of \(M\) are essential. Because \(g\) is convex and the right-hand side is affine, allowing \(z\in[0,1]\) produces a convex continuous relaxation, although its strength depends on how tightly \(M\) bounds \(g\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite valid upper bound converts a binary activation implication into one convex Big-M inequality; relaxing the binary variable remains convex, but loose bounds weaken it.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph lifting of a convex objective function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the restricted epigraph \(E=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:t\geq f(x)\}\). Introducing \(t\) gives \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{(x,t)\in E}t\). assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Lifts
children.top_down_role: Additional-variable representations that separate nonlinear components.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional lifting by auxiliary variables and projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an auxiliary-variable lift is a set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) in variables \((x,y)\), where \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\). It is exact when \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x Q\), equivalently when \(x\in S\) if and only if there exists \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that \((x,y)\in Q\). The lift is convex when \(Q\) is convex, and every objective depending only on \(x\) has the same feasible objective values over \(S\) and \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables form an exact lift when projecting the lifted feasible set onto the original coordinates recovers exactly the original feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the original feasible set.
\(p\geq1\) and \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a specified set in variables \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is an exact lift of \(S\) if and only if \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x Q\).

children.title: Lifted Linking Geometry
children.top_down_role: Coupling relations connecting original variables to lifted components.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Linking Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-valid linking constraints in a finite-dimensional extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the linked lifted set \(\widetilde Q=\{(x,y)\in Q:L(x,y)=0\}\). Its projection is exactly \(S\) if and only if both fiber conditions hold: for every \(x\in S\), there exists \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\) with \((x,y)\in\widetilde Q\), and every \((x,y)\in\widetilde Q\) satisfies \(x\in S\). If \(Q\) is convex and \(L\) is affine, then \(\widetilde Q\) and \(\operatorname{proj}_x\widetilde Q\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linking constraints are exact when every original feasible point has a linked lifted witness and every linked lifted point projects to an original feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the target set.
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a base lifted set.
\(L:\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\to\mathbb{R}^r\) is a specified linking map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x\widetilde Q\) if and only if \(S\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x\widetilde Q\) and \(\operatorname{proj}_x\widetilde Q\subseteq S\).

notation.meaning: Lifted set after imposing the linking equations

children.title: Convex Disjunctive-Hull Formulations
children.top_down_role: Hull-oriented formulations for unions of convex alternatives.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x H=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^k C_i\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact convex alternatives; the formulation represents the convex hull of their union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\lambda C=\{\lambda u:u\in C\}\) for \(\lambda\geq0\), and let \(H\) contain tuples satisfying \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k x_i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), and \(x_i\in\lambda_i C_i\) for every \(i\). Then \(H\) is convex and its projection onto \(x\) is exactly the convex hull of the disjunctive set \(\bigcup_{i=1}^k C_i\). Restricting \(\lambda\) to unit vectors recovers the original union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregate the point across convex alternatives and weight them by simplex variables; projection of the resulting convex formulation is exactly the union’s convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Disjunctive-Hull Formulations

children.title: Extended Conic Lifts
children.top_down_role: Cone-based lifts replacing generic nonlinear representations.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A,B,b\) have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,y):Ax+By+b\in K\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine conic representation and projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended conic lift represents a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) by auxiliary variables and one affine cone-membership condition: \(x\in S\) if and only if there exists \(y\) such that \(Ax+By+b\in K\). The lifted set is convex because it is the affine inverse image of a convex cone, and its projection \(S\) is convex. When a nonlinear epigraph has such a representation, its generic nonlinear inequality may be replaced exactly by this lifted conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set has an extended conic lift when membership is equivalent to the existence of auxiliary variables satisfying an affine cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Conic Lifts

children.title: Lower-Bounding Representation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparison of continuous, polyhedral, conic, and disjunctive lower-bounding representations.

children.title: Continuous NLP Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Cone or function-preserving relaxations obtained by relaxing integrality.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous NLP Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality relaxation of a convex MINLP minimization model while preserving its continuous convex constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=C\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times Z)\) and \(R=C\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\operatorname{conv}(Z))\). Then \(F\subseteq R\), so minimizing the unchanged objective \(c\) over \(R\) gives a lower bound on its infimum over \(F\). If \((x^*,z^*)\) minimizes \(c\) over \(R\) and \(z^*\in Z\), then \((x^*,z^*)\in F\) and it is globally optimal over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing only integrality while preserving the continuous convex constraints enlarges the feasible set and gives a lower bound; an integral optimizer of the relaxation solves the original model.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\) is the feasible set defined by the continuous convex constraints.
\(Z\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^q\) is the discrete-variable domain.
\(c:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is the unchanged minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R\) and \(\inf_{(x,z)\in R}c(x,z)\leq\inf_{(x,z)\in F}c(x,z)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set defined by the preserved continuous constraints

children.title: MILP Outer-Approximation Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral master relaxations generated from convex support information.

knowledge_statements.title: MILP Outer-Approximation Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite tangent-cut MILP relaxation for differentiable convex inequalities in a convex MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{(x,z)\in P\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{Z}^q):g_j(x,z)\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\). For finite sets \(P_j\), define \(R_P\) by retaining \((x,z)\in P\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{Z}^q)\) and imposing \(g_j(\bar w)+\nabla g_j(\bar w)^{\mathsf T}((x,z)-\bar w)\leq0\) for every \(\bar w\in P_j\). Convexity implies \(F\subseteq R_P\). Because the base constraints and cuts are linear and the designated variables remain integral, \(R_P\) is MILP-representable and gives a valid lower bound for the same linear minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At finitely many points, tangent inequalities of differentiable convex constraints form an MILP outer relaxation that preserves every feasible mixed-integer point and yields a minimization lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\) is a nonempty polyhedron, with \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^q\) designated as integer variables.
Each \(g_j\) is differentiable and convex on an open convex set containing \(P\).
Each \(P_j\subseteq P\) is a finite set of linearization points.
The minimization objective is linear and unchanged between the original model and its relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R_P\), and minimizing the common linear objective over \(R_P\) gives a lower bound on minimizing it over \(F\).

notation.meaning: Finite linearization-point set for constraint j
A linearization point in the joint continuous relaxation space

children.title: Mixed-Integer Conic Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Cone-preserving relaxations avoiding full polyhedralization.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the feasible set of a mixed-integer minimization problem.
\(R_K\) retains affine memberships in closed convex cones and relaxes at least one remaining restriction.
The objective \(c\) is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R_K\) and \(\inf_{R_K}c\leq\inf_F c\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex cone used in the representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bounding relaxation that preserves conic structure and may retain integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer conic relaxation is a superset \(R_K\) of \(F\) described by affine constraints, selected integrality restrictions, and conditions of the form \(A_ix+B_iz+b_i\in K_i\), where each \(K_i\) is a closed convex cone. Because \(F\subseteq R_K\), its minimization value is a valid lower bound. Unlike a finite MILP outer approximation, the cone memberships are not replaced by finitely many supporting halfspaces; thus the represented curved convex boundary is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer conic relaxation enlarges the original feasible set while retaining cone constraints, producing a lower bound without finitely polyhedralizing curved convex geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Conic Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound property and cone-preserving distinction are plausible and locally appropriate, but no source is supplied for the mixed-integer conic formulation or its contrast with finite polyhedral outer approximation.

children.title: Activation-Disjunction Strengthening Family
children.top_down_role: Strengthening based on activation structure and convex alternatives.

children.title: Perspective Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Activation-aware convex strengthening based on perspective representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Strengthening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective hull for a bounded on-off convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{(0,0,t):t\geq0\}\cup\{(x,1,t):x\in X,\ t\geq f(x)\}\). Define \(f^{\pi}(x,z)=zf(x/z)\) for \(z>0\), \(f^{\pi}(0,0)=0\), and \(f^{\pi}(x,0)=+\infty\) for \(x\neq0\). Then \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D)=\{(x,z,t):0\leq z\leq1,\ x\in zX,\ t\geq f^{\pi}(x,z)\}\). Consequently, this set is contained in every closed convex relaxation in the same variables that contains \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective inequality and scaled domain describe the closed convex hull of a bounded on-off convex epigraph and therefore give the strongest closed convex relaxation in the same variables.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and contains \(0\).
\(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is closed and convex with \(f(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D)=\{(x,z,t):0\leq z\leq1,\ x\in zX,\ t\geq f^{\pi}(x,z)\}\).

notation.meaning: Closed perspective of the convex function

children.title: Disjunctive Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Convexification based on alternative feasible regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Strengthening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthening a closed convex relaxation by the closed convex hull of a finite disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every closed convex set \(R\) containing \(D\) also contains \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D)\). Hence replacing \(R\) by \(R\cap\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D)\) preserves every point of \(D\) and cannot enlarge the relaxation. If \(D\) is compact, then \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\) is closed and the closure is unnecessary. An exact extended formulation of the closed hull gives the strongest closed convex relaxation of the disjunction in the represented variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a closed convex relaxation with the closed convex hull of its disjunctive alternatives preserves feasible points and can only strengthen the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\bigcup_{i=1}^kD_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a finite disjunctive feasible set.
\(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, and contains \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D)\subseteq R\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex hull of the disjunctive set

children.title: Comparative Relaxation Strength
children.top_down_role: Relative lower-bound quality across perspective, disjunctive, plus combined representations.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2\) are feasible regions for the same minimization objective \(c\).
The three infima are well-defined in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in R_2}c(x)\leq\inf_{x\in R_1}c(x)\leq\inf_{x\in F}c(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion comparison of lower-bounding relaxations for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relaxation \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\) when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\), provided both contain \(F\). Set inclusion implies the displayed ordering of minimization bounds: the stronger relaxation has the larger, hence no worse, lower bound. Strict containment need not produce a strictly better bound for a particular objective. Equality \(R_1=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(F)\) gives the strongest closed convex feasible-set relaxation in the same variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, a contained relaxation is stronger and yields a no-smaller lower bound, though strict set containment need not improve every objective’s bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparative Relaxation Strength

children.title: Formulation Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons involving relaxation strength, auxiliary dimensions, constraint counts, plus master growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size comparison for exact or relaxed lower-bounding formulations of the same convex MINLP set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let formulations \(F_1\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p_1}\) and \(F_2\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p_2}\) use auxiliary variables \(z_1,z_2\), and let \(P_i=\{x:\exists z_i,(x,z_i)\in F_i\}\). If \(P_1=P_2\), both formulations give the same continuous lower bound for every objective depending only on \(x\), although their variable and constraint counts may differ. If \(P_1\subsetneq P_2\), then for minimization \(\inf_{x\in P_1}c^\top x\geq\inf_{x\in P_2}c^\top x\); thus a larger lifted formulation can yield a stronger projected relaxation, and size alone does not order bound quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent projections give identical lower bounds despite different sizes. A larger lifted formulation may project to a tighter relaxation, so formulation size alone does not determine strength.
assumptions_latex: \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are nonempty lower-bounding formulations.
The minimized objective is \(c^\top x\) and is independent of auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1=P_2\) implies equal bounds, while \(P_1\subsetneq P_2\) implies the bound from \(P_1\) is no weaker.

notation.meaning: Projection of formulation i onto the original-variable space.
Number of auxiliary variables in formulation i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection and bound-ordering statements are mathematically correct and the property kind fits the tradeoff leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Solver Compatibility Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representation choices relative to available polyhedral, nonlinear, or conic solver capabilities.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver Compatibility Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of replacing an unsupported convex representation by a solver-compatible relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the feasible set of a convex lower-bounding formulation and let \(R\supseteq S\) be obtained by replacing unsupported nonlinear or conic constraints with constraints accepted by a chosen solver. For every minimization objective \(f\), \(\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\leq\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\). Hence compatibility-preserving replacement remains a valid lower bound only when it enlarges the feasible set; it can weaken that bound. An exact compatible reformulation, characterized by equality of the projected feasible sets, preserves the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing unsupported constraints by a solver-compatible outer relaxation preserves validity but may weaken a minimization bound; an exact projected reformulation preserves it.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(R\) are nonempty and \(S\subseteq R\).
Both formulations use the same minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compatible relaxation has value at most the original lower-bounding formulation, with equality guaranteed by projected equivalence.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the original convex formulation.
Feasible set of the solver-compatible relaxation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-inclusion argument is correct and the principle kind fits the leaf, but the solver-compatibility claim has no cited source.

children.title: Fixed-Integer Subproblem Families
children.top_down_role: Feasible and infeasible continuous subproblems associated with discrete assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Integer Subproblem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous optimization and feasibility subproblems induced by a fixed discrete assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex MINLP \(\min\{f(x,y):g_i(x,y)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\}\), the fixed-integer optimization subproblem at \(\bar y\in Y\) is \(v(\bar y)=\inf\{f(x,\bar y):x\in X,\ g_i(x,\bar y)\leq0\}\). If this set is empty, a fixed-integer feasibility subproblem minimizes a nonnegative violation measure, for example \(\rho(\bar y)=\inf_{x\in X}\max\{0,g_1(x,\bar y),\ldots,g_m(x,\bar y)\}\). The assignment is feasible exactly when \(\rho(\bar y)=0\) and the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing an integer assignment produces either a continuous optimization problem or, when infeasible, a violation-minimization problem used to generate exclusion information.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed and convex, and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^q\).
For every fixed \(y\), the functions \(f(\cdot,y)\) and \(g_i(\cdot,y)\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family consists of \(v(\bar y)\) for feasible assignments and violation problems \(\rho(\bar y)\) for infeasible assignments.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the continuous subproblem at the fixed assignment.
Minimum aggregate constraint violation at the fixed assignment.

review_flags: classical OA subproblem source not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two fixed-assignment subproblem forms are precise, and the attainment qualification correctly handles zero unattained violation infima. A classical OA source is still required.

children.title: OA Master-Formulation Families
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral masters coordinating discrete search and accumulated support information.

knowledge_statements.title: OA Master-Formulation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral epigraph and feasibility masters assembled from accumulated convex supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given sampled points \((x^k,y^k)\), choose subgradients \((a_k,b_k)\in\partial f(x^k,y^k)\) and \((c_{ik},d_{ik})\in\partial g_i(x^k,y^k)\). A standard OA master minimizes \(\eta\) over \(x\in X_P\), \(y\in Y\), and \(\eta\in\mathbb R\), subject to \(\eta\geq f(x^k,y^k)+a_k^\top(x-x^k)+b_k^\top(y-y^k)\) and \(0\geq g_i(x^k,y^k)+c_{ik}^\top(x-x^k)+d_{ik}^\top(y-y^k)\) for retained indices. Variants differ by retained cuts, auxiliary epigraphs, and valid assignment-exclusion constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An OA master is a mixed-integer polyhedral model combining objective epigraph supports, constraint supports, and optional assignment-exclusion constraints accumulated from subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are convex on a convex domain containing all master points.
\(X_P\) is a polyhedral outer representation of the continuous domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every displayed support inequality is globally valid, so the master optimum is a lower bound for the original minimization problem.

notation.meaning: Master epigraph variable for the objective value.
Constraint subgradient for constraint i at sample k.

review_flags: locator supports convex support validity but may not cover OA architecture

children.title: OA Subproblem Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Support and exclusion information returned by fixed-integer subproblems.

children.title: OA Optimality Support
children.top_down_role: Globally valid support information returned by feasible fixed-integer subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: OA Optimality Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subproblem information certifying a globally valid objective underestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^k,y^k)\) solve the fixed-assignment convex subproblem at \(y^k\), and let \((a_k,b_k)\in\partial f(x^k,y^k)\). Convexity certifies \(f(x,y)\geq f(x^k,y^k)+a_k^\top(x-x^k)+b_k^\top(y-y^k)\) throughout the convex modeling domain. Therefore the master inequality \(\eta\geq f(x^k,y^k)+a_k^\top(x-x^k)+b_k^\top(y-y^k)\) is a verifiable global epigraph underestimator. At \((x^k,y^k)\) it is tight, with right-hand side \(f(x^k,y^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient at a solved fixed-assignment point gives a globally valid objective underestimator that is tight at that point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper convex and subdifferentiable at \((x^k,y^k)\).
The OA master ranges only over the convex domain on which the subgradient inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed epigraph inequality is globally valid and exact at \((x^k,y^k)\).

notation.meaning: Objective epigraph variable in the OA master.
A subgradient of the objective at the sampled point.

children.title: OA Feasibility Exclusion
children.top_down_role: Information used to exclude or refine infeasible discrete assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: OA Feasibility Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual or no-good information certifying exclusion of an infeasible discrete assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed assignment \(\bar y\), suppose there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) such that \(\delta:=\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x,\bar y)>0\). Then no \(x\in X\) satisfies all inequalities \(g_i(x,\bar y)\leq0\), because such an \(x\) would make the weighted sum nonpositive. Thus \((\lambda,\delta)\) certifies infeasibility and permits exclusion of \(\bar y\). If \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^q\), the valid no-good inequality is \(\sum_{j:\bar y_j=0}y_j+\sum_{j:\bar y_j=1}(1-y_j)\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive weighted infeasibility bound certifies that a fixed assignment has no feasible continuous completion; for binary variables, a no-good inequality excludes it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the continuous domain and \(g_i(x,\bar y)\leq0\) are the fixed-assignment constraints.
The lower bound \(\delta>0\) is computed or certified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment \(\bar y\) is infeasible and may be removed by a valid assignment-exclusion constraint.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative multiplier vector forming the infeasibility aggregate.
Strictly positive lower bound on the aggregate violation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both the positive weighted infeasibility certificate and binary no-good inequality are correctly stated, but no source supports this OA certificate record.

children.title: OA Certificate Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convexity, duality, plus solver-status regimes governing certificate reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: OA Certificate Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which subproblem-derived supports remain globally valid in the master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An OA certificate generated at \(z^k=(x^k,y^k)\) is globally valid on a master domain \(D\) precisely when its affine function \(\ell\) has the required global relation there: \(\ell(z)\leq f(z)\) for an objective epigraph cut, or \(\ell_i(z)\leq g_i(z)\) for a constraint cut used as \(\ell_i(z)\leq0\). Convex subgradients guarantee these relations on convex \(D\); conic dual separation guarantees analogous halfspaces when the dual certificate has the correct cone sign. A merely local derivative without such structure is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An OA certificate is valid only when its affine support globally underestimates the represented convex function, or follows from a correctly signed conic separator.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) contains every point admissible to the OA master.
Each certificate is evaluated using the same representation from which it was derived.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global validity is equivalent to the required support inequality holding for every \(z\in D\).

notation.meaning: Domain searched by the OA master.
Affine function encoded by an OA certificate.

review_flags: conic portion needs a dedicated source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-support validity condition is correct, but the conic portion does not introduce a cone, mapping, or precise sign convention and lacks a dedicated source. Source-backed specification is needed before the combined regime can be accepted.

children.title: Smooth Convex Validity Regime
children.top_down_role: Globally supporting linearizations for differentiable convex representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Validity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine supports generated by gradients of differentiable convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and convex. For every base point \(\bar x\in D\), the first-order model \(\ell_{\bar x}(x)=g(\bar x)+\nabla g(\bar x)^\top(x-\bar x)\) satisfies \(\ell_{\bar x}(x)\leq g(x)\) for all \(x\in D\). Consequently, the inequality \(\ell_{\bar x}(x)\leq0\) contains the convex feasible set \(\{x\in D:g(x)\leq0\}\) and is a globally valid OA constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable convex constraint, its tangent affine function is a global underestimator, so the linearized inequality is a valid outer approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is open and convex.
\(g\) is differentiable and convex on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\bar x)+\nabla g(\bar x)^\top(x-\bar x)\leq g(x)\) for every \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: First-order affine model of g at the base point.
Convex domain on which global validity is asserted.

children.title: Nonsmooth Convex Validity Regime
children.top_down_role: Globally supporting outer models supplied by valid subgradient information.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex Validity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine supports generated by valid subgradients of nonsmooth convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(g:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, and choose \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\) with \(s\in\partial g(\bar x)\). By the defining subgradient inequality, \(g(x)\geq g(\bar x)+s^\top(x-\bar x)\) for every \(x\in D\). Hence \(g(\bar x)+s^\top(x-\bar x)\leq0\) is a globally valid OA relaxation of \(g(x)\leq0\), without requiring differentiability or uniqueness of \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any valid subgradient of a proper convex constraint defines a global affine underestimator and therefore a valid OA inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper and convex on the convex set \(D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Conic OA Validity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid outer halfspaces obtained from dual-cone elements and cone separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^r\) be a closed convex cone and consider the conic constraint \(F(x)=Ax+b\in K\). For any \(u\in K^*=\{u:u^\top v\geq0\text{ for all }v\in K\}\), every feasible point satisfies \(u^\top(Ax+b)\geq0\). Thus \(u\) certifies the globally valid OA halfspace \(u^\top(Ax+b)\geq0\). If a trial image \(F(\bar x)\notin K\) is strictly separated from \(K\) by such a \(u\) with \(u^\top F(\bar x)<0\), the halfspace excludes \(\bar x\) while retaining every conically feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-cone vector yields a valid linear inequality for every conically feasible point and can separate an infeasible trial point.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(F(x)=Ax+b\) is affine.
The certificate satisfies \(u\in K^*\), with the stated sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^\top(Ax+b)\geq0\) is globally valid for \(Ax+b\in K\) and excludes \(\bar x\) when \(u^\top F(\bar x)<0\).

children.title: Global-Validity Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representations for which local linear models are not global outer approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Validity Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonconvex constraint whose tangent inequality excludes feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=1-x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and impose \(g(x)\leq0\), whose feasible set is \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\). At the feasible base point \(\bar x=1\), the affine linearization is \(g(1)+g'(1)(x-1)=-2(x-1)\). Enforcing this linearization as \(-2(x-1)\leq0\) gives \(x\geq1\), which excludes every feasible point \(x\leq-1\). Therefore a tangent inequality from a differentiable but nonconvex constraint need not be a global outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the nonconvex constraint 1−x²≤0, linearization at x=1 excludes the entire feasible branch x≤−1, demonstrating failure of global OA validity.
assumptions_latex: The tangent inequality is used without convexity, a valid convex underestimator, or spatial localization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linearized set \([1,\infty)\) does not contain the original feasible set \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\).

notation.meaning: Nonconvex constraint function in the counterexample.

children.title: Exact Master–Subproblem Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Master–Subproblem Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of classical convex OA with exact solves and finitely many assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a convex MINLP with finite discrete set \(Y\). Assume every fixed-assignment continuous subproblem and every OA master is solved exactly; valid objective and feasibility certificates are added; each infeasible assignment is excluded; and every feasible assignment either supplies its exact value or is not revisited without a strictly improved bound. If the continuous subproblems attain their optima and the constraint qualification needed for their OA certificates holds, then after at most finitely many assignment evaluations the algorithm either certifies infeasibility or returns an assignment and continuous solution attaining the global MINLP optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finitely many assignments, exact master and subproblem solves, valid certificates, and assignment exclusion, convex OA terminates finitely at a global optimum or infeasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is finite, and fixed-assignment subproblems are convex and attain their optima.
Masters and subproblems are solved exactly, with globally valid certificates.
Previously resolved assignments cannot cycle without bound improvement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The OA procedure terminates after finitely many assignment evaluations with a global optimum or an infeasibility certificate.

notation.meaning: Finite set of admissible discrete assignments.

review_flags: classical convex OA finite-convergence theorem source not supplied

children.title: Discrete-Assignment Exclusion Regime
children.top_down_role: Termination organized through certified treatment of finitely many discrete assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Assignment Exclusion Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-assignment bound for convex OA with certified subproblems and permanent exclusion of processed assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a finite set of discrete assignments. At iteration \(k\), select an assignment \(y^k\in Y\) not previously processed, solve its continuous subproblem with a certificate of infeasibility or certified optimal solution, and add all required valid outer-approximation cuts. Then impose a no-good constraint excluding \(y^k\). Because no assignment can recur, the method performs at most \(|Y|\) certified continuous-subproblem evaluations. If the master is solved exactly and termination occurs only when its valid lower bound meets the incumbent value, exhaustion or bound closure certifies global optimality or infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permanent exclusion after certified treatment prevents repeated assignments, giving at most one continuous-subproblem evaluation per discrete assignment and finite global termination under exact master bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is finite.
Every processed subproblem returns a valid optimality or infeasibility certificate.
Master lower bounds and exclusion constraints are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of certified subproblem evaluations is at most \(|Y|\), and bound closure certifies the global result.

notation.meaning: finite set of admissible discrete assignments

children.title: Inexact Subproblem Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Subproblem Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification conditions under which approximate continuous solves preserve OA bounds and exclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each assignment \(y\), let \(v_y\) denote the exact continuous-subproblem value. An inexact oracle is admissible when it returns either a rigorous infeasibility certificate or bounds \(L_y\le v_y\le U_y\), together with affine minorants that remain globally valid after explicitly certified error offsets. It may trigger exclusion of \(y\) only after infeasibility is certified or after all information required from that assignment has been generated with errors included in the master and incumbent bounds. A stopping test is reliable only if the resulting global lower and upper bounds retain their stated directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate subproblem solves are safe only when their errors are certified, propagated into cuts and bounds, and never used to exclude a potentially feasible or improving assignment.
assumptions_latex: Each fixed-assignment continuous problem is convex.
Reported value and cut errors have rigorous finite bounds.
Discrete assignments belong to a finite set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certified inexactness preserves valid OA lower and upper bounds; uncontrolled inexactness does not.

notation.meaning: exact value of the continuous subproblem at assignment y
certified lower and upper enclosures of the subproblem value

children.title: Numerical Tolerance Regime
children.top_down_role: Stopping behavior controlled by feasibility, optimality, plus integrality tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Tolerance Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap and feasibility tolerances interpreted through certified error-adjusted bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat L\) and \(\widehat U\) be computed master and incumbent values with certified errors \(e_L,e_U\ge 0\). Define \(L=\widehat L-e_L\) and \(U=\widehat U+e_U\), provided that \(L\) is a valid global lower bound and a certificate establishes an exactly feasible solution whose objective value is at most \(U\). Stop only when \(U-L\le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}\). A point having constraint residual at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{feas}}\) may contribute to \(U\) only through a certified exactly feasible repair or another rigorous certificate of a feasible objective upper bound. Cut-generation errors may contribute to \(L\) only when their allowances preserve global validity of the master relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination tolerances certify a gap only when outward error adjustments preserve a valid global lower bound and an upper bound backed by an exactly feasible solution or a rigorous feasible-repair certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(e_L,e_U\ge 0\) are rigorous error allowances.
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{feas}}\ge 0\).
The adjusted value \(L\) is a valid global lower bound, and the adjusted value \(U\) bounds the objective of a certified exactly feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certified absolute optimality gap is at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}\).

notation.meaning: certified global lower and upper bounds

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: outward error adjustment is necessary for a rigorous numerical optimality gap

children.title: Termination Reliability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Situations where accumulated numerical error weakens a claimed completion certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination Reliability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single false exclusion destroys the global guarantee, even for a finite convex instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(X=\{0\}\), \(Y=\{0,1\}\), and the convex MINLP \(\min\{y:(x,y)\in X\times Y\}\). Its unique optimal assignment is \(y=0\), with value \(0\). If an inexact subproblem routine falsely reports assignment \(y=0\) infeasible and OA permanently excludes it, the remaining master returns \(y=1\) with value \(1\). Thus no positive feasibility or solver tolerance, by itself, preserves finite-convergence correctness: every permanent exclusion must follow a valid infeasibility certificate or another logically sufficient certified treatment of the assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even one erroneous infeasibility declaration can remove the unique optimum; permanent assignment exclusion therefore requires certification, not merely a numerical solver status.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm permanently excludes assignments declared infeasible.
An inexact oracle may issue one false infeasibility declaration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite enumeration alone cannot guarantee correctness when a false exclusion is possible.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Tree Outer Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical OA with a separately solved master at every outer iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a polyhedral master \(M_0\), incumbent value \(U=+\infty\), and iteration \(k=0\). Solve \(M_k\) to obtain a lower bound \(L_k\) and discrete assignment \(y^k\). Solve the convex continuous subproblem at \(y^k\); if feasible, update \(U\) and add valid objective and constraint supporting cuts, and if infeasible, add a valid feasibility cut. Exclude \(y^k\) when its certified treatment is complete, form \(M_{k+1}\), and solve this new master as a separate optimization tree. Stop when \(U-L_k\) meets the prescribed certified gap or the master is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multi-tree OA alternates complete master solves with fixed-assignment convex subproblems, rebuilding or restarting the master search after each new batch of cuts.

Subproblem cuts and infeasibility conclusions are valid.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize one branch-and-cut search for a valid mixed-integer linear outer relaxation. For a feasible solve, update the incumbent and insert globally valid objective and constraint linearizations; for a certified infeasible solve, insert a valid feasibility or no-good cut. Reject the current candidate whenever a new cut separates it, but retain the same search tree and its unaffected nodes. Terminate only when the branch-and-cut lower bound and the certified incumbent satisfy the required gap, or when the tree proves the relaxation infeasible.

Callback processing occurs before an integer candidate is accepted.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Outer Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: OA candidate selection stabilized by a regularizer without changing the certified relaxation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the current OA master feasible set \(M_k\), center \(\bar z^k\), regularizer \(R_k(z,\bar z^k)\ge0\), and parameter \(\rho_k\ge0\), select the next candidate by solving \(\min\{\eta+\rho_kR_k(z,\bar z^k):(z,\eta)\in M_k\}\).
