knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global lower bound obtained by convexifying the discrete domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the minimization problem with feasible set \(F\subseteq X\times Y\), where \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\). Let \(R\subseteq X\times\operatorname{conv}(Y)\) be a convex set satisfying \(F\subseteq R\), and let \(f\) agree with the original objective on \(F\). If the convex relaxation is solved with certified value \(L_R=\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in R\}\), then \(L_R\) is a globally valid lower bound on the original optimal value \(z^*=\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing over a convex superset of the mixed-integer feasible region produces a globally valid lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
The relaxation satisfies \(F\subseteq R\).
The value \(L_R\) is computed or bounded rigorously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R\ \Longrightarrow\ L_R=\inf_R f\leq\inf_F f=z^*.\)

children.title: Polyhedral Master Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Master Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound from a polyhedral outer master containing valid underestimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_M\supseteq Y\) be a master domain and suppose every accumulated cut \(\theta\geq\alpha_k+\beta_k^{\mathsf T}y\) underestimates the feasible objective value for each original assignment \(y\in Y\). Include only feasibility cuts valid for all feasible assignments, and define \[L_M=\inf\{\theta:y\in Y_M,\ \theta\geq\alpha_k+\beta_k^{\mathsf T}y\ (k\in K),\ y\text{ satisfies all feasibility cuts}\}.\] If the master retains every original feasible assignment with its attainable objective value, then \(L_M\leq z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral master built from valid objective underestimators and feasibility cuts yields a global lower bound when it relaxes every feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: Every objective cut is a valid underestimator on the original discrete domain.
Every feasibility cut is valid for all feasible assignments.
The master optimization value is certified globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_M\leq z^*.\)

notation.meaning: index set of accumulated objective cuts

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Feasible Incumbent Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-bound certificate furnished by any feasible mixed-integer point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*=\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in F\}\) be the value of a minimization problem. For any verified feasible point \((\hat x,\hat y)\in F\), define \(U=f(\hat x,\hat y)\). Feasibility makes \(U\) a globally valid upper bound: \(z^*\leq U\). For a collection of verified feasible points \(S\subseteq F\), the incumbent value \(U_S=\min\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in S\}\) remains a valid upper bound and is no larger than the value of any member of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective value of any verified feasible solution is a global upper bound; the best such value is the incumbent bound.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
Every point used to update the incumbent is verified feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\hat x,\hat y)\in F\ \Longrightarrow\ z^*\leq f(\hat x,\hat y)=U.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Discrete-Search Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality after exhaustive certified treatment of a finite assignment set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the discrete domain \(Y\) be finite, and let \(U\) be the value of a verified feasible incumbent. Suppose every \(y\in Y\) has been certified either infeasible for the continuous subproblem or incapable of improving the incumbent, meaning a valid subproblem lower bound \(L(y)\) satisfies \(L(y)\geq U\). Then no feasible discrete–continuous solution has objective below \(U\). Consequently, the incumbent is globally optimal. If every assignment is instead certified infeasible and no incumbent exists, the original problem is globally infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite discrete domain, certifying every assignment infeasible or unable to beat the incumbent completes the global search.
assumptions_latex: The discrete assignment set \(Y\) is finite.
Every assignment receives a rigorous infeasibility certificate or valid lower bound.
The incumbent, when present, is verified feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\forall y\in Y:\ y\text{ infeasible or }L(y)\geq U\bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ z^*=U.\)

notation.meaning: valid lower bound for the subproblem at assignment y

knowledge_statements.title: Global Bound-Gap Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-relative optimality certificate from globally valid lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(L\) be a globally valid lower bound and let \(U\) be the objective value of a verified feasible incumbent, so \(L\leq z^*\leq U\). Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\geq0\), termination is certified when \[U-L\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}.\] The incumbent then satisfies \(0\leq U-z^*\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}\), under this stated absolute-relative accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a feasible upper bound and global lower bound differ by at most the chosen tolerance, the incumbent is certified approximately optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is globally valid and satisfies \(L\leq z^*\).
\(U\) comes from a verified feasible incumbent.
Both tolerances are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}\ \Longrightarrow\ U-z^*\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\max\{1,|U|\}.\)

Let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) be the finite discrete search domain and let \(X(y)\) be the feasible region of the continuous subproblem fixed at \(y\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract semantics for interpreting solver results independently of vendor-specific status names.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a model instance \(M\), define the semantics of a solver result \((s,\tau,d)\) as the set
\[\Sigma(s,\tau,d,M)=\{q:q\text{ is a mathematical claim validated by }M,\tau\text{ and the returned data }d\}.\]
Thus a label such as optimal, infeasible, or unbounded has no standalone mathematical force: its meaning is conditioned on the solved model, termination mode, feasibility and optimality tolerances, residuals, bounds, and any certificate data. A downstream component may assert only claims belonging to \(\Sigma(s,\tau,d,M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver status means only the mathematical claims supported by its model, termination metadata, tolerances, residuals, bounds, and returned certificate data.

children.title: Mathematical Certificate Semantics

assumptions_latex: A claim domain \(\mathcal Q\), witness domain \(\mathcal W\), and deterministic verifier are specified.
The verifier evaluates the original mathematical model rather than an undocumented solver state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A certificate \(C=(q,w)\) is valid exactly when \(V(M,q,w)=1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifier-based semantics for certificates exchanged between decomposition components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a mathematical model \(M\), a certificate is a pair \(C=(q,w)\in\mathcal Q\times\mathcal W\), where \(q\) is a precise claim and \(w\) is its witness. Its semantics are determined by a declared verifier
\[V:\mathcal M\times\mathcal Q\times\mathcal W\to\{0,1\}.\]
The certificate is valid exactly when \(V(M,q,w)=1\). Typical claims include primal feasibility, infeasibility of a fixed-assignment subproblem, validity of a lower bound, or optimality within a stated tolerance. A status label without a witness or independently validated numerical conditions is not itself such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mathematical certificate is a precise claim plus a witness, and it is valid exactly when a declared verifier accepts both against the original model.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Solver Status Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound normalization of heterogeneous solver results into common certificate claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a model \(M\) and raw result \(r_k\) from solver \(k\). Initialize the canonical outcome to \(\mathsf{unknown}\). Decode the source status, termination reason, tolerances, primal and dual residuals, bounds, and witness data. For each candidate canonical claim \(q\), construct a witness \(w\) and evaluate the common verifier \(V(M,q,w)\). Set
\[T_k(M,r_k)=q\quad\text{only if}\quad V(M,q,w)=1.\]
If exactly one candidate passes validation, emit that claim; otherwise emit \(\mathsf{unknown}\). Stop after exhausting the claims associated with the decoded source result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decode each solver's complete result and emit a canonical claim only when exactly one candidate passes common validation; otherwise return unknown.
assumptions_latex: Each source solver exposes its raw result schema and tolerance conventions.
A common canonical claim set and validators are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The translator emits \(q\) only when it is the unique validated candidate; otherwise it emits \(\mathsf{unknown}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary for status translation when the translator's complete observation underdetermines a mathematical claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(o\) denote all information available to a translator, including the exposed model representation, raw status, termination metadata, tolerances, residuals, bounds, and witness data. Suppose two compatible executions produce the same observation \(o\), while the valid canonical claim is \(q_I\) in one execution and \(q_U\) in the other. No translator using only \(o\) can soundly emit either claim in both cases. Its sound canonical result is therefore
\[T(o)=\mathsf{unknown},\]
unless additional information distinguishes the executions and validates one claim.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: state components indexed by changed variables, constraints, or solver internals lose their mathematical interpretation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary beyond which source solver state has no well-defined target interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a source state component \(z^s\) be indexed or interpreted by model \(M^s\). Transfer is compatible only if there exists a declared mapping \(\Phi\) into \(M^t\) that preserves dimensions and the mathematical object represented by \(z^s\). If a variable is eliminated, a constraint is reordered or rescaled without metadata, an inequality reverses orientation, or the active-set representation changes, then the identity copy generally lacks this property. In that case
\[\Phi(z^s)\text{ is undefined},\]
and using the copied component as target state has no valid warm-start semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State cannot be copied when changed variables, constraints, scaling, orientation, or internal schemas destroy its source-to-target mathematical interpretation.
knowledge_statements.title: Transfer Compatibility Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits and the qualification about absent metadata is important, but the asserted compatibility boundary requires an implementation or solver-interface source.

children.title: Callback Lazy-Cut Integration Interface
children.top_down_role: Event-driven nonlinear separation inside a branch-and-cut tree.

children.title: Nonlinear Separation Callbacks
children.top_down_role: Event-driven interfaces for nonlinear violation detection within the MILP tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Separation Callbacks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient separation of violated convex nonlinear constraints at a callback candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a candidate \((\widehat x,\widehat y)\). Initialize an empty cut set and evaluate each designated convex nonlinear constraint. Whenever \(g_i(\widehat x,\widehat y)>0\), choose \(s_i\in\partial_x g_i(\widehat x,\widehat y)\) and emit
\[g_i(\widehat x,\widehat y)+s_i^{\mathsf T}(x-\widehat x)\le 0.\]
Each emitted inequality is valid for every \(x\) satisfying \(g_i(x,\widehat y)\le 0\) and excludes \(\widehat x\). Stop after all designated constraints have been tested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a candidate, linearize each violated convex constraint with a subgradient and return the resulting globally valid separating cuts.
assumptions_latex: For the fixed discrete assignment \(\widehat y\), each function \(g_i(\cdot,\widehat y)\) is convex and subdifferentiable at \(\widehat x\).
The callback is invoked at a candidate \(\widehat x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every emitted cut is valid for all \(x\) satisfying \(g_i(x,\widehat y)\le 0\) and separates \(\widehat x\) when \(g_i(\widehat x,\widehat y)>0\).

children.title: Lazy-Cut Integration
children.top_down_role: Insertion of deferred globally valid constraints at eligible tree events.

assumptions_latex: Each submitted lazy cut is valid for every feasible solution represented by the active callback context.
The solver enforces every accepted lazy cut before accepting an incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding the cuts removes no feasible solution and rejects any incumbent that violates a submitted separating cut.

notation.meaning: set defined by submitted lazy cuts

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: globally valid inequalities preserve the feasible set, while enforced separating cuts exclude violating incumbents
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness condition for integrating callback-generated inequalities as lazy constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be the feasible set of the original MINLP and let each submitted lazy inequality be \(a_k^{\mathsf T}z\le b_k\). Valid integration requires
\[F\subseteq L:=\bigcap_k\{z:a_k^{\mathsf T}z\le b_k\}.\]
Hence replacing the current relaxation \(R\) by \(R\cap L\) preserves every point of \(F\). If an incumbent \(\widehat z\) satisfies \(a_k^{\mathsf T}\widehat z>b_k\) for a submitted cut, enforcing that cut rejects \(\widehat z\). Correctness additionally requires the solver to process accepted lazy cuts before declaring the incumbent feasible or terminating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy cuts are safe only when valid for every original feasible point and enforced before a violating incumbent can be accepted.
knowledge_statements.title: Lazy-Cut Integration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly states the feasible-set preservation condition for lazy cuts and fits the integration leaf, but no solver-interface or optimization source supports the enforcement requirement.

children.title: Callback Event Regimes
children.top_down_role: Root, node, incumbent, plus relaxation events available for nonlinear refinement.

assumptions_latex: The solver identifies callback events and the mathematical status of their candidate points.
Permitted callback actions are declared for each event class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An action is admissible only when its validity predicate holds in the current event regime.

notation.meaning: validity predicate for action a at event e

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: callback admissibility depends on whether the event exposes an integer incumbent, fractional relaxation point, or heuristic context
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-indexed admissibility of separation, rejection, and heuristic actions during MILP search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition callback invocations into event regimes such as integer-incumbent, fractional-relaxation, and heuristic-solution events. For event \(e\) with candidate \(z_e\), an action \(a\) is admissible exactly when
\[P(e,a,z_e)=1,\]
where \(P\) includes both mathematical validity and the solver's event contract. Incumbent rejection may use a constraint valid for all feasible integer solutions; modification of a node relaxation requires an inequality valid on the relaxation domain claimed by the interface; a heuristic event may propose a point but cannot certify it. Actions lacking a declared predicate value are inadmissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Callback actions are permitted only when both their mathematical validity and the solver contract hold for the current event type and candidate.
knowledge_statements.title: Callback Event Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the event-regime leaf, but callback permissions are solver-interface-specific and require a source defining the relevant event contracts.

children.title: Callback Validity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Solver restrictions or cut-scope conditions limiting event-driven integration.

knowledge_statements.title: Callback Validity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes globally valid callback cuts from node-local restrictions in a minimization decomposition solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the original feasible set and let \(Q_v\) be the region represented by callback node \(v\). A generated inequality \(h(x)\le 0\) may be inserted globally only if \(h(x)\le 0\) for every \(x\in F\). It may be inserted locally at \(v\) if \(h(x)\le 0\) for every \(x\in F\cap Q_v\). The validity boundary is crossed when a merely local inequality is installed globally: if some \(x^*\in F\setminus Q_v\) satisfies \(h(x^*)>0\), the modified global master excludes an originally feasible point and may return an invalid optimum or infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A callback cut is globally admissible only when valid for every original feasible point; promoting a merely node-local cut can destroy correctness.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the unchanged feasible set of the original problem.
\(Q_v\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the callback node region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global insertion is sound only if \(F\subseteq\{x:h(x)\le 0\}\); local insertion at \(v\) requires only \(F\cap Q_v\subseteq\{x:h(x)\le 0\}\).

notation.meaning: Region associated with callback node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the global-versus-node-local validity distinction is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the callback event and insertion semantics.

children.title: Persistent Incremental Solver Interface
children.top_down_role: Incremental modification and state preservation across iterations or nodes.

children.title: Persistent Solver Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Long-lived solver models preserving internal state across repeated solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Solver Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface contract for retaining a solver instance across successive master-model updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A persistent solver interface for models \(M_k\) is a stateful map maintaining a solver state \(S_k\) and exposing operations \(\operatorname{attach}(M_0)\), \(\operatorname{update}(U_k)\), and \(\operatorname{solve}()\). If \(M_{k+1}=U_k(M_k)\), the update operation must produce a state \(S_{k+1}\) whose represented optimization model is mathematically equivalent to \(M_{k+1}\), without requiring reconstruction of the solver object. Retained algorithmic data, such as incumbents, bases, or search information, are optional and may affect execution but not the feasible set, objective, or declared solution status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent interface updates one live solver instance while ensuring that its represented model remains equivalent to the intended updated model.
assumptions_latex: Each \(M_k\) has a well-defined feasible set and objective.
Each accepted update \(U_k\) has specified model semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After every accepted update, \(\operatorname{model}(S_{k+1})\equiv M_{k+1}\).

notation.meaning: Optimization model at update index k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but persistence, reconstruction, retained-state, and solution-status guarantees vary by solver interface and have no cited support.

children.title: Incremental Model Modification
children.top_down_role: Localized changes to variables, constraints, bounds, objectives, or cut pools.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Model Modification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transactional update procedure for a persistent MILP master used by a decomposition method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a represented model \(M_k\), persistent state \(S_k\), and a finite update list \(U_k=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\). First validate that every \(u_i\) is supported and that all referenced variables, constraints, and parameters exist. Apply the updates transactionally to obtain \(M_{k+1}=u_r\circ\cdots\circ u_1(M_k)\), synchronize the solver representation, and invalidate any retained state whose documented assumptions are changed. If validation or synchronization fails, restore \(M_k\) and \(S_k\). Otherwise output \(S_{k+1}\) only after verifying that its variables, constraints, bounds, and objective represent \(M_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate and apply supported updates atomically, invalidate incompatible retained state, and commit only when the live solver represents the intended model.
assumptions_latex: \(S_k\) represents \(M_k\) before the transaction.
The interface identifies its supported update classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either returns \(S_{k+1}\) with \(\operatorname{model}(S_{k+1})\equiv M_{k+1}\), or leaves \((M_k,S_k)\) unchanged.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but atomic rollback, synchronization verification, and state invalidation are interface-dependent requirements unsupported by a source.

children.title: State-Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solver capabilities governing retention of bases, factorizations, presolve state, or search information.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Preservation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies persistent-solver updates by the amount of reusable algorithmic state retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an update from \(M_k\) to \(M_{k+1}\), classify the transition by the retained-state set \(R_{k+1}\subseteq S_k\). In the cold regime, \(R_{k+1}=\varnothing\) and the updated model is solved from a fresh algorithmic state. In the warm regime, \(R_{k+1}\) contains only explicitly imported hints, such as an incumbent or basis. In the persistent regime, the solver retains additional compatible internal search state. In every regime, preserved data must satisfy the interface's compatibility predicate for \(M_{k+1}\); otherwise those data must be discarded. Under correct synchronization, all three regimes represent the same updated optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cold, warm, and persistent regimes retain progressively more compatible solver state, but must represent the same updated mathematical model.
assumptions_latex: \(S_k\) is the algorithmic state obtained while processing \(M_k\).
The interface supplies a compatibility predicate for retained data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each regime, \(\operatorname{model}(S_{k+1})\equiv M_{k+1}\), while \(R_{k+1}\) determines only the retained algorithmic information.

notation.meaning: Subset of prior state retained after updating

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role is suitable, but the cold, warm, and persistent classification and the asserted compatibility predicate are not established by cited literature or interface documentation.

children.title: Incremental-Update Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Model modifications that preserve or invalidate reusable solver state.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental-Update Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate connecting a model update with reusable persistent-solver state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) transform model \(M\) into \(M'=U(M)\), and let \(R\) be solver state proposed for reuse. The pair \((U,R)\) is incrementally compatible when: the interface implements every elementary change in \(U\); synchronization yields a solver representation equivalent to \(M'\); every datum in \(R\) remains well-defined under the new variable and constraint mapping; and reusing \(R\) cannot suppress any feasible solution, required search region, or correctness check for \(M'\). If any clause fails, compatibility requires discarding the affected state or rebuilding the solver representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An update is compatible only when it is supported, synchronized exactly, and all reused state remains semantically safe for the new model.
assumptions_latex: \(M'=U(M)\) has defined mathematical semantics.
\(R\) is identifiable independently of the updated model representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds exactly when supported synchronization gives \(\operatorname{model}(S')\equiv M'\) and reuse of \(R\) preserves solver correctness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the proposed necessary-and-sufficient compatibility clauses depend on solver-specific update and retained-state semantics for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Outer-Model Management
children.top_down_role: Policies governing the generation, retention, scaling, and scope of convex support information.

children.title: Cut Insertion Policy Family
children.top_down_role: Policies for staged, selective, aggregated, or comprehensive cut insertion.

children.title: Cut Selection Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies prioritizing candidate cuts by violation, strength, diversity, or expected utility.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Selection Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Score-and-filter rule for choosing globally valid cuts before insertion into an outer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a relaxation point \(\bar x\), a finite pool \(C\\) of valid inequalities \(a_i^Tx\le b_i\), a selection budget \(q\), and tolerances \(\varepsilon,\delta\ge0\). For each cut compute violation \(v_i=(a_i^T\bar x-b_i)_+\) and normalized efficacy \(e_i=v_i/\max\{\lVert a_i\rVert_2,\delta\}\). Remove cuts with \(v_i\le\varepsilon\), duplicates, and cuts dominated according to the declared dominance test. Rank the remainder by a fixed score formed from efficacy and any declared diversity or sparsity terms. Output at most \(q\) highest-ranked cuts, with deterministic tie-breaking. Selection never changes the validity requirement on admitted cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filter invalidly weak, duplicate, or dominated candidates, score the rest, and select a budgeted set without relaxing cut validity.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(C\) is valid for the original feasible set.
\(q\in\mathbb Z_+\) and the ranking rule is fixed before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(B\subseteq C\) satisfies \(|B|\le q\) and contains only cuts with \(v_i>\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the statement contains malformed LaTeX after the cut-pool symbol and permits an undefined efficacy value when both the row norm and delta are zero. A sourced policy and a positive-denominator condition are required.

children.title: Cut Batching Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies controlling grouped, staged, aggregated, or comprehensive cut insertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Batching Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accumulation rule controlling when selected cuts are committed to the outer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input selected-cut sets \(B_t\), a pending buffer \(P_t\), batch capacity \(m\in\mathbb Z_+\), and maximum delay \(d\in\mathbb Z_+\). Update \(P_{t+1}=P_t\cup B_t\), removing duplicates. Commit a batch when \(|P_{t+1}|\ge m\), when the oldest buffered cut has waited \(d\) iterations, or when a termination or synchronization event requires an exact current outer model. At commitment, insert every cut in \(P_{t+1}\) atomically and reset the buffer to the empty set. Before any claimed final certificate, flush all pending correctness-relevant cuts required by the declared decomposition protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Buffer selected cuts until a size, delay, synchronization, or termination trigger occurs, then insert the batch atomically.
assumptions_latex: Each \(B_t\) contains cuts admissible for the outer model.
Iteration indices are discrete and ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every buffered cut is either committed within \(d\) iterations or explicitly discarded under the declared selection policy before certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the certification flush rule and maximum-delay guarantee are decomposition-protocol dependent and unsupported. The timing convention also needs specification to make the within-d-iterations conclusion precise.

children.title: Selection–Batching Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance among master growth, reoptimization cost, plus refinement strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Batching Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates mathematical relaxation strength from implementation cost when selecting and batching valid cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(C)=\{x\in R_0:a_i^Tx\le b_i\text{ for every }i\in C\}\) be a minimization relaxation formed from valid cuts. If \(C_1\subseteq C_2\), then \(R(C_2)\subseteq R(C_1)\), so their relaxation values satisfy \(z(C_1)\le z(C_2)\le z^*\). Consequently, selecting or committing more valid cuts cannot weaken the current lower bound. Delaying a cut keeps the weaker relaxation until commitment, whereas inserting larger batches reduces synchronization frequency but enlarges each modified model. The inclusion and bound relations are mathematical; no universal ordering of total runtime follows from them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More committed valid cuts tighten a minimization relaxation, while delayed or larger batches trade synchronization frequency against model size without guaranteeing faster runtime.
assumptions_latex: All cuts in \(C_2\) are valid for the original feasible set.
Both relaxations minimize the same objective over \(R_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C_1\subseteq C_2\), then \(R(C_2)\subseteq R(C_1)\) and \(z(C_1)\le z(C_2)\le z^*\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation after committing cut set C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits and the relaxation-inclusion inequalities are standard for a minimization relaxation, but no cited source supports the combined selection, batching, synchronization, and runtime tradeoff statement.

children.title: Cut Lifecycle Control
children.top_down_role: Policies controlling inactive, dominated, or redundant support information.

children.title: Cut Aging Metrics
children.top_down_role: Activity, slack, recency, plus usefulness signals for support information.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Aging Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-based inactivity measures for cuts retained in a decomposition master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an active cut \(c_i:a_i^Tx\le b_i\) and master solutions \(x^t\), define slack \(s_i^t=b_i-a_i^Tx^t\). Given an activity tolerance \(\tau\ge0\), its consecutive inactivity age is initialized by \(A_i^{t_i}=0\) at insertion time \(t_i\) and updated by \(A_i^{t+1}=0\) when \(s_i^{t+1}\le\tau\), and \(A_i^{t+1}=A_i^t+1\) otherwise. A windowed activity metric may additionally record \(W_i^t=\sum_{j=\max\{t_i,t-w+1\}}^t\mathbf 1\{s_i^j\le\tau\}\). These metrics describe observed use, not logical validity or deletion safety.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut's age counts consecutive iterations of nonactivity; windowed activity counts near-binding occurrences and does not itself prove deletion is safe.
assumptions_latex: Each recorded \(x^t\) satisfies the current master constraints.
Slack is measured after a fixed normalization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_i^t\) measures consecutive nonactivity, while \(W_i^t\) measures activity frequency over the chosen window.

notation.meaning: Slack of cut i at iteration t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but cut age, activity tolerance, normalization, and window conventions are implementation-specific and lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Cut Deletion Policies
children.top_down_role: Removal policies for inactive, dominated, redundant, or numerically harmful cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Deletion Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Age-based deletion rule constrained by protection and certificate-safety requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input the active cut set \(C_t\), protected subset \(P_t\), inactivity ages \(A_i^t\), deletion threshold \(T\), and deletion budget \(r\). Form eligible cuts \(E_t=\{i:c_i\in C_t\setminus P_t,\ A_i^t\ge T\}\). Exclude any cut whose removal would contradict the declared node, bound, or certificate bookkeeping. Rank the remaining eligible cuts by decreasing age and a fixed secondary score, and delete at most \(r\) of them. After deletion, invalidate relaxation values or warm-start data that depended on the removed rows and recompute them before they support pruning or termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete only sufficiently stale, unprotected cuts within a budget, then invalidate and recompute any bounds or state that depended on them.
assumptions_latex: Every protected cut belongs to \(P_t\).
The implementation tracks which bounds and certificates depend on removable cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deleted set \(D_t\) satisfies \(D_t\subseteq C_t\setminus P_t\), \(|D_t|\le r\), and \(A_i^t\ge T\) for every \(i\in D_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but protection, deletion eligibility, dependency tracking, and mandatory recomputation behavior are method-specific and unsupported by a source.

children.title: Protected Cut Classes
children.top_down_role: Certificate-critical or structurally essential cuts retained despite inactivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Protected Cut Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines lifecycle classes exempt from routine cut aging and deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(t\), the protected set \(P_t\subseteq C_t\) consists of active cuts assigned a nondeletable lifecycle class by the decomposition protocol. Such classes include cuts required to preserve an exact base formulation, cuts referenced by an unreleased pruning or infeasibility certificate, and cuts whose regeneration is not guaranteed before their information is needed. Routine age- or efficacy-based deletion must act only on \(C_t\setminus P_t\). A cut may leave \(P_t\) only after every dependent certificate is discharged and the protocol establishes that removal preserves the correctness invariants used by subsequent bounds and termination tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Protected cuts are exempt from routine deletion because the formulation, stored certificates, or future correctness currently depends on them.
assumptions_latex: \(C_t\) is the active cut set.
Certificate and formulation dependencies are explicitly tracked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Routine deletion candidates must lie in \(C_t\setminus P_t\), and protection may be removed only after all stated dependencies are discharged.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but the listed protected classes and conditions for releasing protection depend on the decomposition protocol and certificate implementation; no supporting citation is provided.

children.title: Deletion-Safety Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where removing support information weakens validity, reproducibility, or termination evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion-Safety Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when cut removal remains a valid relaxation change and when stale bookkeeping makes it unsound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq R(C)\) be the original feasible set inside a minimization relaxation defined by valid cuts \(C\). Deleting \(D\subseteq C\) gives \(R(C)\subseteq R(C\setminus D)\), so the new relaxation remains valid and its lower bound may decrease. Deletion becomes unsafe if the algorithm retains a bound, fathoming decision, or infeasibility certificate derived from \(R(C)\) while treating it as certified for the weaker model \(R(C\setminus D)\). In particular, any closed node whose pruning depended on a deleted cut must be revalidated or reopened unless its certificate remains valid independently of that cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing valid cuts preserves relaxation validity but can invalidate stored bounds or pruned nodes unless all cut-dependent conclusions are recomputed or revalidated.
assumptions_latex: Every cut in \(C\) is valid for \(F\).
The problem is a minimization problem and deleted-cut dependencies are identifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Safe deletion requires revalidation of every dependent conclusion; otherwise a retained pruning or termination certificate can be invalid despite \(F\subseteq R(C\setminus D)\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation induced by active cuts C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and deletion weakens the represented relaxation, but the assertion that every pruning conclusion depending on a deleted globally valid cut must be reopened or revalidated is too broad: deletion of the row does not by itself invalidate a sound mathematical certificate derived from a valid inequality. Precise method-specific certificate semantics require a source.

children.title: Cut Numerical-Quality Control
children.top_down_role: Numerical treatment of support information before master insertion.

children.title: Cut Coefficient Scaling
children.top_down_role: Normalization of support coefficients before outer-model insertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Coefficient Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive row normalization for linear cuts, distinguishing exact normalization from floating-point storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In exact arithmetic, given a nonzero cut \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\), set \(s=\max\{\lVert a\rVert_\infty,|b|\}>0\), \(\widehat a=a/s\), and \(\widehat b=b/s\). Then \(\widehat a^{\mathsf T}x\le\widehat b\) if and only if \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\), and \(\max\{\lVert\widehat a\rVert_\infty,|\widehat b|\}=1\). When the scaled coefficients are rounded for floating-point storage, exact halfspace preservation is not automatic and requires a separately justified validity policy. Coefficient deletion is likewise a separate operation and must not be treated as normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact positive row normalization preserves a cut and gives unit maximum coefficient magnitude; floating-point rounding or coefficient deletion requires a separate validity policy.
assumptions_latex: The exact cut is \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\), where \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\).
The normalization identity is interpreted in exact arithmetic; floating-point storage is treated separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In exact arithmetic, the normalized inequality represents the same halfspace and has maximum coefficient magnitude equal to \(1\); floating-point preservation requires additional justification.

children.title: Outer-Model Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Numerical quality of the accumulated master representation.

assumptions_latex: The outer model has linear constraint matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
Diagonal row and column scalings are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A scaling is numerically acceptable only when it reduces coefficient imbalance without changing the exact represented feasible set.

notation.meaning: Positive diagonal row and column scalings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal equilibration criterion for a linear outer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive diagonal matrices \(D_r\) and \(D_c\), define \(\widetilde A=D_rAD_c\) and substitute \(x=D_c\widetilde x\), scaling each constraint and its right-hand side by the corresponding diagonal entry of \(D_r\). The conditioning regime is acceptable when the transformed model is algebraically equivalent to the original and a declared imbalance measure, such as the ratio of largest to smallest nonzero row norms, is reduced. Bounds, objective coefficients, integrality declarations, and recovered primal solutions must be transformed consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer-model conditioning uses consistent positive row and variable scaling to reduce coefficient imbalance while preserving constraints, bounds, integrality, and solution recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Model Conditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic scaling is plausible, but the declared acceptability criterion and implementation requirements need a numerical-optimization source with a specific locator.

children.title: Scaling Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling choices relative to solver tolerances, coefficient ranges, plus certificate interpretation.

assumptions_latex: The original model uses variables \(x\), and the scaled model uses \(z\) with \(x=Dz+d\).
The diagonal entries of \(D\) are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaling is compatible precisely when every generated cut and every solver tolerance is interpreted through the same invertible transformation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of variable scaling, cut generation, and feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(x=Dz+d\), a cut \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) is represented in scaled coordinates by \((D^{\mathsf T}a)^{\mathsf T}z\le b-a^{\mathsf T}d\). A scaling regime is compatible when this transformation is applied to every cut, bounds are mapped componentwise, integer variables are left unscaled or transformed by an integrality-preserving bijection, and feasibility tolerances are converted to measure the same residual convention. In that regime, cut satisfaction in either coordinate system is equivalent before numerical tolerances are applied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling is compatible when cuts, bounds, integrality, and residual tolerances all follow one invertible coordinate transformation.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Compatibility Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine cut transformation is correct, but the claimed precise compatibility condition, especially integrality and solver-tolerance conversion, is implementation-sensitive and unsourced.

children.title: Numerical Degradation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Poorly scaled or nearly dependent cuts that undermine stable master solves.

assumptions_latex: Cut activity is tested in floating-point arithmetic with unit roundoff \(u\).
A stored cut is \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\).

children.title: Globally Valid Cut Scopes

assumptions_latex: The original feasible set is \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
A cut is represented by an inequality \(\ell(x)\le0\).

The cut has global scope when \(F\subseteq H_\ell\), equivalently when \(\ell(x)\le0\) for every \(x\in F\). Such a cut may be imposed at every node or region whose feasible points are contained in \(F\), without excluding any feasible solution of the original problem.

It may be enforced only in subproblems whose admissible domains are contained in \(R\). Local validity imposes no requirement on feasible points in \(F\setminus R\), so the cut cannot be installed globally without an additional validity certificate.

The original feasible set is \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Promotion to scope \(S\) is valid if and only if \(F\cap S\subseteq\{x:\ell(x)\le0\}\).

Promotion to global scope is the special case \(S=\mathbb R^n\); observed validity at sampled points is not a certificate.

children.title: Scope-Misclassification Boundary
children.top_down_role: Invalid inference caused by treating locally valid information as globally valid.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(F\), and a cut \(\ell(x)\le0\) is valid only on \(R\).
The cut is incorrectly enforced on a larger region \(S\supsetneq R\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by assigning a local cut to an unsupported larger scope.

Thus the boundary between harmless and correctness-destroying scope assignment is precisely whether \(F\cap S\) remains contained in the cut halfspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For parameter \(y\in[-2,2]\), define the projected value \(\phi(y)=\min\{(x^2-1)^2:x=y\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex projected quartic value function has a tangent at zero that lies above its value at one, invalidating convex Benders support.

children.title: Primal Attainment Failures

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Attainment Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-valued convex problem whose infimum exists but is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the convex problem \(p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R} e^x\). Its feasible set is nonempty and its objective is continuous and strictly convex. Because \(e^x>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), while \(e^{x_k}\to0\) for \(x_k=-k\), one has \(p^*=0\) but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=\varnothing\). Thus finite optimal value, feasibility, and convexity do not ensure primal attainment on a noncompact feasible set; a decomposition subproblem may return arbitrarily accurate minimizing sequences without an optimizer from which to generate an attained-point certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous convex problem on a noncompact set can have a finite infimum but no optimizer, leaving decomposition with only minimizing sequences.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R\)
The objective is \(f(x)=e^x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=0\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin} f=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attainment Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-gap convex example in which no finite Lagrange multiplier attains the dual supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^*=\min\{x:x^2\le0,\ x\in\mathbb R\}\). The sole feasible point is \(x=0\), so \(p^*=0\). For multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\), the dual function is \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}(x+\lambda x^2)\), hence \(q(0)=-\infty\) and \(q(\lambda)=-1/(4\lambda)\) for \(\lambda>0\). Consequently \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=0=p^*\), but no finite \(\lambda\) attains \(d^*\). The failure coincides with absence of a strictly feasible point.

Lagrange multipliers satisfy \(\lambda\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex and continuous. Suppose \(x^*\in X\) attains the finite minimum of \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). If there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}X\) such that \(g_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i\), then some \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb R_+^m\) attains the Lagrange-dual optimum, the duality gap is zero, \(\lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\) for every \(i\), and \(0\in\partial f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^*\partial g_i(x^*)+N_X(x^*)\). Thus \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) is an attained KKT certificate. Without an applicable constraint qualification, such multiplier attainment is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional convex problem with continuous objective and constraint functions, an attained optimum and Slater's condition yield an attained dual multiplier, zero duality gap, and a KKT certificate; without an applicable qualification, multiplier recovery is not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Certificate Effectiveness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation threshold distinguishing valid dual certificates that strengthen a master relaxation from those that do not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(y)\) be a subproblem value function and let a dual certificate generate a valid support \(\ell_\lambda(y)\le v(y)\). At a master candidate \((\bar y,\bar\eta)\), the certificate is separating exactly when \(\ell_\lambda(\bar y)>\bar\eta\); adding \(\eta\ge\ell_\lambda(y)\) then removes that candidate. The equality \(\ell_\lambda(\bar y)=\bar\eta\) is the effectiveness boundary. If \(\ell_\lambda(\bar y)<\bar\eta\), the certificate remains mathematically valid but supplies no separation at the candidate. If \(\ell_\lambda(\bar y)=-\infty\), it supplies no finite lower-bound cut there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid dual cut is effective only when it strictly violates the current master candidate; equality is the exact separation boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_\lambda(y)\le v(y)\) on the master domain.
The master uses the epigraph variable \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut separates \((\bar y,\bar\eta)\) if and only if \(\ell_\lambda(\bar y)>\bar\eta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Open-Domain Boundary Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open convex domain permits finite boundary limits without feasible boundary points or attained minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(0,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=x\) for \(x\in D\). Then \(D\) is convex but not closed, \(f\) is convex and continuous on \(D\), and \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=0\). Nevertheless, no \(x\in D\) attains this value because the limiting point \(0\) lies in \(\overline D\setminus D\). Thus a sequence \(x_k\downarrow0\) may converge to a finite boundary value while the original-domain evaluation and any certificate requiring a feasible base point at \(0\) remain unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex domain, a finite boundary limit can equal the infimum even though no feasible boundary point or optimizer exists.

The objective is \(f(x)=x\) on \(D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Undefined-Domain Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convention separating infeasibility from legitimate finite function and oracle evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex with effective domain \(D=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\). For \(x\notin D\), the optimization value is \(f(x)=+\infty\), not an unspecified finite number, and \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\). Consequently no finite objective value, gradient, or subgradient support based at that point is defined. Any implementation that evaluates a finite-valued formula outside \(D\) without an explicitly valid extension changes the mathematical model and may generate invalid decomposition cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside a proper convex function’s effective domain, its value is infinite and its subdifferential empty; finite oracle evaluations require a justified extension.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain conditions under which a subgradient support is defined and globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex, let \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and choose \(s^0\in\partial f(x^0)\). For a finite constant \(M\in\mathbb R\), the big-M inequality \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\) represents the inactive state \(z=0\) without excluding any \(x\in D\) if and only if \(M\ge M^*:=\sup_{x\in D}g(x)\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact, weak, and invalid big-M constants through inactive-domain extrema.

children.title: Missing or Unstable Subgradient Information
children.top_down_role: Inadequate support information for nonsmooth convex separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing or Unstable Subgradient Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine supports for nonsmooth convex separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the support error by \[\varepsilon(x,\widehat g):=\sup_{z\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x)+\widehat g^{\mathsf T}(z-x)-f(z)\bigr).\] A usable inexact support requires \(\varepsilon(x,\widehat g)<+\infty\), equivalently \(\widehat g\in\partial_{\varepsilon(x,\widehat g)}f(x)\). Subgradient information is missing when every oracle candidate has infinite support error. It is unstable at \(x\) when there are \(x_k\to x\) and returned \(\widehat g_k\) for which \(\varepsilon(x_k,\widehat g_k)\to+\infty\) or \(\|\widehat g_k\|_2\to+\infty\); the associated affine cuts then lack uniformly controlled error or coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A returned vector is usable only if it defines a finite-error global affine support. Infinite support error or exploding vectors under small perturbations indicate missing or unstable subgradients.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and an oracle returns \(\widehat g\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite \(\varepsilon(x,\widehat g)\) certifies \(\widehat g\in\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)\); an infinite residual or unbounded residuals under vanishing input perturbations mark missing or unstable support information.

children.title: Cone-Boundary Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Weak or unstable certificates near singular conic boundary geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone with dual cone \(K^*\).
\(s\in K\) and \(z\in K^*\) are complementary primal and dual vectors, so \(\langle s,z\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vanishing primal and dual boundary margins identify a degenerate conic certificate for which fixed absolute perturbations can change feasibility or facial classification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal-dual conic certificates near proper-face boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonzero complementary vectors define normalized boundary margins \[\mu_K(s):=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(s,\partial K)}{\max\{1,\|s\|_2\}},\qquad \mu_{K^*}(z):=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial K^*)}{\max\{1,\|z\|_2\}}.\] Cone-boundary degeneracy occurs along certificates \((s_k,z_k)\) when \(\mu_K(s_k)\to0\) and \(\mu_{K^*}(z_k)\to0\). For perturbations whose absolute size is comparable to either margin, membership in the relevant cone face is not robust: a perturbed slack may leave \(K\), and a perturbed dual vector may cease to certify the same supporting face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary primal and dual vectors become boundary-degenerate when both normalized distances to their cone boundaries vanish, making facial and feasibility classifications sensitive to small perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Boundary Degeneracy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the proposed margins do not characterize exceptional degeneracy: nonzero complementary vectors in a proper cone generally lie on their respective boundaries, making both distances zero even for ordinary complementary pairs. A source-backed facial, strict-complementarity, or conditioning criterion is required.

children.title: Premature Cone Polyhedralization
children.top_down_role: Loss of strength or excessive model growth from replacing cone structure too early.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed, nonpolyhedral convex cone.
\(P_q=\{u:a_i^{\mathsf T}u\ge0,\ i=1,\ldots,q\}\) is a finite outer approximation satisfying \(K\subseteq P_q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite outer polyhedralization of nonpolyhedral \(K\) is strict and can admit cone-infeasible relaxation points; exactness requires refinement or preservation of the cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite outer approximations of nonpolyhedral cone constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(K\) is nonpolyhedral, no finite halfspace system equals it; hence \(K\subsetneq P_q\) for every finite \(q\). Thus some \(\bar u\in P_q\setminus K\) satisfies every retained linear inequality while violating the original cone constraint. Replacing \(u\in K\) by \(u\in P_q\) before decomposition can therefore yield a strictly weaker relaxation bound or select a cone-infeasible discrete assignment. Exact recovery requires adaptive separation until the incumbent lies in \(K\), or retention of the original conic constraint; fixing \(q\) prematurely provides neither guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite outer polyhedral approximation cannot equal a nonpolyhedral cone. Used too early, it admits cone-infeasible points and may weaken decomposition bounds unless refined adaptively.
knowledge_statements.title: Premature Cone Polyhedralization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and every finite polyhedral outer approximation of a nonpolyhedral cone is necessarily strict. The claims about discrete assignments and exact adaptive recovery are algorithm-dependent and need a targeted cone-decomposition source.

children.title: Feasibility-Classification Failures
children.top_down_role: False feasibility or infeasibility near solver tolerances.

assumptions_latex: Constraints are \(g_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\) and \(h_j(x)=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\).
The numerical classifier uses an absolute feasibility tolerance \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tolerance feasibility differs from exact feasibility precisely on accepted points with \(0<r(x)\le\tau\); an infeasibility declaration additionally requires a valid global certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based classification of nonlinear subproblem feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[r(x):=\max\bigl\{0,\max_i g_i(x),\max_j|h_j(x)|\bigr\},\qquad X:=\{x:r(x)=0\}.\] A classifier accepting \(x\) whenever \(r(x)\le\tau\) produces false exact feasibility for every accepted point with \(0<r(x)\le\tau\). Conversely, failure to find a point satisfying \(r(x)\le\tau\) does not imply \(X=\varnothing\). Declaring infeasibility from that failure alone is invalid; an exact or tolerance-qualified global infeasibility certificate is required. Hence near-tolerance residuals must be reported separately from certified feasibility or infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residuals between zero and the solver tolerance are numerically feasible but not exactly feasible. Failure to find such a point is not, by itself, an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Classification Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits and the residual-based distinction between exact and tolerance feasibility is mathematically sound. The required form of an infeasibility declaration or certificate depends on solver status semantics and needs a specific source.

children.title: Cross-Solver Tolerance Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Conflicting master, NLP, separation, and integrality tolerances.

assumptions_latex: The master accepts a candidate when its maximum cut violation is at most \(\tau_M\).
The separator returns a violated cut only when its violation exceeds \(\tau_S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonempty tolerance gap exists whenever \(\tau_M<\tau_S\), permitting points that the master rejects but the separator cannot separate.

notation.meaning: Maximum cut violation at a candidate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency between master acceptance and separation decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a candidate has maximum relevant violation \(v\ge0\). If \(\tau_M<\tau_S\), every value \[\tau_M<v\le\tau_S\] lies in a classification gap: the master does not accept the candidate, while the separator returns no violated cut. Repeated encounters with this gap can prevent either acceptance or progress. A sufficient compatibility rule for these two decisions is \(\tau_S\le\tau_M\), together with a common residual scaling. Analogous interfaces between NLP feasibility, integrality, and cut validation require conversion to the same scaled residual before their tolerances are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the separator threshold exceeds the master tolerance, some candidates are rejected by the master yet generate no cut. Compatible scaling and ordered tolerances remove this decision gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Solver Tolerance Inconsistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the stated gap follows under the explicitly given master and separator decision rules. The sufficiency claim and extensions to NLP and integrality interfaces require a sourced common-scaling protocol.

children.title: Master Cycling-Conditioning Failure Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cycling and numerical degradation caused by weak, redundant, or poorly scaled support information.

children.title: Repeated Discrete Assignments
children.top_down_role: Recurrence of previously evaluated integer configurations during decomposition.

assumptions_latex: The discrete assignment set \(Y\) is finite.
A decomposition method generates a sequence \((y^k)_{k\ge0}\subseteq Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An infinite run necessarily repeats an assignment; recurrence without an exclusion, strengthening, or state-changing update constitutes discrete cycling.

notation.meaning: Indices of two visits to one assignment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycling of finite-domain master assignments in decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A repeated discrete assignment occurs when \(y^k=y^\ell\) for some \(k<\ell\). Because \(Y\) is finite, every infinite assignment sequence contains an assignment occurring infinitely often. Such recurrence is a cycling failure when processing \(y^k\) adds no constraint excluding it, no strictly stronger valid support at that assignment, and no persistent state change that alters its future evaluation. A finite-termination architecture must therefore ensure that each revisited assignment is either certified final or subjected to a monotone update that cannot recur indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any infinite sequence over finitely many assignments repeats. Repetition becomes cycling when revisiting an assignment neither certifies it nor adds a persistent exclusion or strengthening.
knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Discrete Assignments

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits. Finite-set recurrence is correct, but the characterization of cycling and the asserted finite-termination requirement depend on the decomposition state and anti-cycling mechanism; a targeted algorithmic source is needed.

children.title: Redundant Support Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Growth of duplicated or nearly duplicated support information in the master problem.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(k\), the master region is \(M_k=\{x\in M_0:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,k\}\).
Each added inequality is valid for the original optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(M_k=M_{k-1}\), cut \(k\) is redundant; indefinitely many such equalities cause model growth without relaxation strengthening.

notation.meaning: Master feasible region after k cuts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact redundancy in accumulated linear master supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The new support \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\le b_k\) is redundant relative to the current master exactly when \[M_{k-1}\subseteq\{x:a_k^{\mathsf T}x\le b_k\},\] equivalently \(M_k=M_{k-1}\). Redundant support accumulation occurs along an unbounded index set \(I\) for which this equality holds while every retained cut remains in the master. Then the number of rows grows with \(|I|\), but neither the feasible region nor the relaxation bound changes because of those rows. Duplicate positive scalings of an existing inequality are a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A newly added support is redundant when the previous master already implies it. Retaining indefinitely many such cuts enlarges the model without changing its region or bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Support Accumulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the exact redundancy equivalence is correct for the stated master regions. No citation supports the cut-accumulation failure interpretation or cut-management context.

children.title: Master Problem Scaling Deterioration
children.top_down_role: Loss of numerical balance across master constraints, variables, or generated support information.

knowledge_statements.title: Master Problem Scaling Deterioration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient and row scaling of evolving linear master problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonzero rows \(a_{ki}^{\mathsf T}\) define \[\rho_k:=\frac{\max_i\|a_{ki}\|_2}{\min_i\|a_{ki}\|_2},\qquad \delta_k:=\frac{\max_{i,j}|(A_k)_{ij}|}{\min_{i,j:(A_k)_{ij}\ne0}|(A_k)_{ij}|}.\] Master scaling deteriorates along the decomposition sequence if \(\rho_k\to+\infty\) or \(\delta_k\to+\infty\). These ratios measure representation-dependent disparities rather than intrinsic problem difficulty: positive row rescaling can change them without changing the exact feasible set. Consequently, scaling deterioration is a numerical failure diagnostic, not by itself a proof of mathematical ill-posedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Master scaling deteriorates when row norms or nonzero coefficient magnitudes develop unbounded ratios. This is representation-dependent and signals numerical risk rather than mathematical ill-posedness.
assumptions_latex: \(A_kx\le b_k\) is the linear constraint system of the master at iteration \(k\).
Every nonzero row of \(A_k\) has finite Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Divergence of row-norm or coefficient dynamic range is a scaling-deterioration diagnostic and precedes any claim about intrinsic conditioning.

notation.meaning: Master constraint matrix at iteration k
Ratio of largest to smallest nonzero row norm
Ratio of largest to smallest nonzero coefficient magnitude

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Master Systems
children.top_down_role: Solver instability attributable to poorly conditioned master representations.

assumptions_latex: A master linear or quadratic solve produces a square system \(K_kw_k=d_k\).
The condition number is measured in the Euclidean operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Singular \(K_k\) or diverging \(\kappa_2(K_k)\) identifies an ill-conditioned master-system family with potentially unbounded relative sensitivity.

notation.meaning: Master basis, normal-equation, or KKT matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of basis, normal-equation, or KKT systems in the master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K_k\) is nonsingular, define \[\kappa_2(K_k):=\|K_k\|_2\|K_k^{-1}\|_2=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(K_k)}{\sigma_{\min}(K_k)}.\] The master system is singular when \(\sigma_{\min}(K_k)=0\), and a sequence is increasingly ill-conditioned when \(\kappa_2(K_k)\to+infty\). For the perturbed right-hand side \(d_k+e_k\), the solution perturbation is \(K_k^{-1}e_k\); hence directions associated with \(\sigma_{\min}(K_k)\) amplify errors by the factor \(1/\sigma_{\min}(K_k)\). Large residual accuracy can therefore coexist with unreliable primal, dual, or cut coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master system is singular when its smallest singular value is zero and increasingly ill-conditioned when its condition number diverges, allowing small data errors to strongly perturb solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Master Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the singular-value and condition-number formulas are correct. The concluding claims about relative sensitivity and reliability of primal, dual, or cut coefficients require specified perturbation scaling and a numerical linear-algebra source.
